topics.title: Risk and reward
topics.summary: Investors who lend or buy shares want to be paid for waiting and for taking risk, and that payment is exactly what a firm must pay to raise capital. This topic links the investor's required return to the firm's cost of capital, explains risk aversion and the risk premium, and summarises what a century of market history says about risk and reward.

topics.title: Measuring return and risk
topics.summary: Return is measured by the expected (mean) return and risk by the standard deviation. You compute both from states of the economy with probabilities, or from a history of returns using the population or sample formula, then use the normal distribution to turn them into ranges and probabilities and plot each stock on a risk-return diagram.

topics.title: Two-stock portfolios
topics.summary: A portfolio's expected return is a simple weighted average, but its risk is not: it depends on how the two stocks move together, measured by correlation. Whenever the correlation is below 1 the portfolio is less risky than the weighted average of the two risks, and adding more and more stocks reduces risk toward the limit set by the market itself.

concepts.term: Required return and cost of capital
concepts.definition: The expected return E[R] that investors need for bearing a given amount of risk. From the investor's (lender's) side it is the required rate of return; from the firm's (borrower's) side the same number is the cost of capital.
concepts.explain: Money flows from investors to firms, and the interest rate or return in between is both the reward of one side and the cost of the other. Investments of similar risk should offer similar returns, so a project is judged against the return investors require for projects of its own risk. This is why the whole chapter is about measuring risk and the reward it earns.
concepts.example: Investors in comparable pipeline bonds require 6.1% per annum. Bow River Pipelines must offer about 6.1% to raise money for a line of the same risk, so 6.1% is its cost of capital: a line expected to earn only 5.4% should be rejected. For shares, R = D1/P0 + g: D1 = $1.976, P0 = $38.00, g = 4% gives R = 5.2% + 4% = 9.2%.
concepts.contrast: Required return is forward-looking and tied to risk; a realized return is what actually happened and can be far above or below it. Cost of capital is what investors demand, not the accounting interest a firm paid last year or a project's own IRR (which is compared with it).
concepts.trap: Do not treat the risk-free rate (or a project's own return) as the discount rate: the benchmark is the return required for the project's risk. Watch for 'similar risk', 'cost of capital' and 'required return' as cue words: they all point to the same number seen from two sides.
concepts.mnemonic: One rate, two views: the lender's reward is the borrower's cost.
concepts.formula: E[R] = R_F + risk premium; R = D1/P0 + g

concepts.term: Risk aversion and the risk premium
concepts.definition: People are risk averse when they want compensation for taking on higher risk; the risk premium (excess return) is that compensation, E[R] − R_F, the expected return above the risk-free rate.
concepts.explain: Risk aversion does not mean people refuse risk; it means they take risk only when paid for it. The premium is measured against the risk-free asset (T-bills): for a stock the equity risk premium is the expected stock return minus the T-bill rate. Historically it is estimated as the average stock return minus the average T-bill return over the same years.
concepts.example: T-bills pay 2% and the stock market is expected to return 8%, so the equity risk premium is 8% − 2% = 6%. Historically, a stock that averaged 11.0% while T-bills averaged 3.9% earned a premium of 11.0% − 3.9% = 7.1% per annum.
concepts.contrast: Risk averse: needs compensation for higher risk. Neutral toward risk: needs none, only E[R] matters. Risk seeking: will accept less expected return to take risk. 'Risk averse' is not 'risk avoiding'. Risk premium is not the stock's total return.
concepts.trap: Subtract the risk-free rate from the expected return (not the other way round, not the latest T-bill rate if the question gives a series: use the average over the same years). Ex ante premiums are positive; realized premiums over a short sample can be negative.
concepts.mnemonic: Premium = pay for risk = E[R] − R_F.
concepts.formula: risk premium = excess return = E[R] − R_F

concepts.definition: Over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the text) small-company stocks beat large-company stocks, which beat long-term bonds, which beat T-bills. Lesson 1: risky assets on average earn a risk premium. Lesson 2: the greater the potential reward, the greater the risk (standard deviation). Real returns come from the Fisher relationship.
concepts.explain: Higher average returns went hand in hand with higher volatility: small stocks paid most and swung most. The averages hide big year-to-year swings, so a risk premium is not a guarantee in any single year. Nominal returns must be converted to real returns with (1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real), not by simple subtraction.
concepts.example: Large-company stocks averaged 12.0% (σ 19.9%) and T-bills 3.4% (σ 3.1%), a premium of 8.6%. With inflation averaging 3.0%, the real T-bill return was 1.034/1.030 − 1 ≈ 0.4% per year, and the real return on small stocks was 1.166/1.03 − 1 = 13.2%.
concepts.contrast: Lesson 1 (a positive average premium for risk) versus Lesson 2 (more reward comes with more risk). Nominal versus real return: the nominal return includes inflation. T-bills are nearly free of default risk but not of inflation risk.
concepts.trap: Subtracting inflation from the nominal rate is only an approximation; the exam rewards the Fisher division (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf) − 1. One bad year does not contradict the premium: premiums are long-run averages.
concepts.mnemonic: Stocks > bonds > bills; small > large; more reward, more risk.

concepts.term: Expected return from states of the economy
concepts.definition: E[R] = Σ p_i R_i: the probability-weighted average of an asset's returns R_i across the states i, where the probabilities p_i add to 1. For a portfolio, find the portfolio return in each state first, or use E[R_P] = Σ w_k E[R_k].
concepts.explain: When we forecast returns for scenarios such as boom, normal and recession, we weight each scenario by how likely it is. The result is an average, not a promise: it may not equal any single state's return. Equal probabilities reduce it to the simple average, which is also what a historical mean does.
concepts.contrast: Forecast states use probabilities p_i; a historical mean uses weights 1/N. E[R] (reward) is not σ (risk). The expected return is not the most likely return.
concepts.trap: Probabilities must add to 1 (find a missing one as 1 minus the others). Keep the sign of negative returns. Do not use the simple average when the probabilities differ, and do not divide by N − 1 (no N − 1 with probabilities).

concepts.term: Variance and standard deviation from states
concepts.definition: σ² = Σ p_i (R_i − E[R])², the probability-weighted average of squared deviations from the expected return; σ = √σ² is the standard deviation, the measure of total (volatility) risk, in the same units as returns.
concepts.explain: Standard deviation tells us how widely outcomes are spread around the expected return. Compute E[R] first, then the deviation in each state, square it, weight by the probability, add, and take the square root. The risk-free asset has σ = 0 because its return is the same in every state.
concepts.contrast: Variance σ² is in squared units (0.0139); standard deviation σ is its square root (11.78%) and is what we plot. With forecast probabilities there is no N − 1; N − 1 belongs to the sample variance of historical returns.
concepts.trap: Do not stop at the variance, do not divide by N − 1, do not square the returns instead of the deviations, and keep units consistent (decimals with decimals, or percents throughout). For a portfolio compute the portfolio's return in each state first; never average the stocks' σ's.

concepts.term: Historical mean and standard deviation (population vs sample)
concepts.definition: For N past returns, E[R] = μ = (R_1 + … + R_N)/N. The population standard deviation divides the sum of squared deviations by N; the sample standard deviation divides by N − 1. Use population when the data are the entire group (all stocks in your portfolio), sample when they are a sample (five years of your favourite stock).
concepts.explain: With history every observation counts equally, so no probabilities appear. The sample formula divides by N − 1 because the deviations are measured from the sample's own mean, which would otherwise understate the spread. The sum of the deviations from the mean is always zero, a handy check.
concepts.example: A stock returned 12%, −4%, 18%, 7%, 9% over five years (a sample). Mean = 8.4%; squared deviations sum to 261.2; variance = 261.2/4 = 65.3; σ = 8.08%. Treated as a population, 261.2/5 = 52.24 and σ = 7.23%.
concepts.contrast: Population (÷N) versus sample (÷(N − 1)): the sample σ is slightly larger. Historical (equal weights, ÷N or N − 1) versus states with probabilities (weights p_i, no N − 1). Standard deviation (percent) versus variance (percent squared).
concepts.trap: The question says which one applies ('a sample of five years', 'all nine stocks'): follow it. Using N for a sample or N − 1 for a population are the two classic errors. Report σ in percent, not the variance, and use the average of the T-bill series (not the last year) for historical premiums.
concepts.mnemonic: Sample is N minus one; the whole group is N.

concepts.definition: A symmetric bell-shaped distribution completely described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. About 68% of outcomes fall within μ ± 1σ, about 95% within μ ± 2σ and about 99% within μ ± 3σ. Probabilities for other cut-offs come from z = (X − μ)/σ and the cumulative normal table N(z), with N(−z) = 1 − N(z).
concepts.explain: Annual returns are roughly mound-shaped and symmetric, so we use the normal as an approximation. Two numbers (μ and σ) are enough to give ranges ('two years in three') and the probability of a loss. The table sheet gives N(z) for positive z only; for negative z subtract from 1.
concepts.example: U.S. large-company stocks (1926-2016): μ = 12.0%, σ = 19.9%, so about 68% of years are between −7.9% and 31.9%. For μ = 9.0%, σ = 15.0%, P(loss) = N(−0.60) = 1 − 0.7257 = 27.43%.
concepts.contrast: Within ±1σ (68%) is not the same as below μ − σ (about 16%, half of the 32% outside). The normal is an approximation to actual returns, not an exact description.
concepts.trap: Pick the right multiple (1, 2 or 3 σ) for 68/95/99; centre the range on the mean; for lower-tail probabilities use 1 − N(|z|); for 'between' use N(z_upper) − N(z_lower). Divide by σ, not σ².

concepts.term: Risk-return diagram, domination and the efficient frontier
concepts.definition: A graph with σ (risk, volatility) on the horizontal axis and E[R] (return) on the vertical axis, where each dot is one stock. A stock dominates another if it has a higher E[R] for the same σ, a lower σ for the same E[R], or both. The efficient frontier is the set of points that nothing dominates, along the upper-left boundary.
concepts.explain: To answer 'how do we measure risk and return of a stock', compute E[R] and σ from past returns (for example the last five years) and plot the dot. Up and to the left is better. Stocks off the frontier can be beaten, so only the frontier matters; which frontier stock an investor chooses depends on risk preference. The risk-free asset sits on the vertical axis at R_F.
concepts.example: Tamarack (σ 14%, E 8%), Birchmount (14%, 11%), Quill (10%, 8%): Birchmount and Quill each dominate Tamarack; neither dominates the other because Birchmount offers more return but more risk.
concepts.contrast: Domination compares two points; the efficient frontier is the set of undominated points. The risk-return diagram has σ on the x-axis; the security market line (next chapter) has β on the x-axis.
concepts.trap: Do not confuse the axes; higher E[R] with higher σ is a trade-off, not domination. Equal E[R] with lower σ is domination. Past performance does not guarantee future returns.

concepts.term: Portfolio weights and expected portfolio return
concepts.definition: The weight of asset k is w_k = dollars in k ÷ total dollars invested, so Σ w_k = 1 (a borrowed amount makes a weight negative). The expected return of the portfolio is the weighted average E[R_P] = Σ w_k E[R_k], which is linear.
concepts.explain: Weights come from dollar values, and the portfolio return is just the weighted average of the assets' expected returns, so it always lies between the lowest and highest asset returns. A risk-free asset is part of the portfolio with its own weight and return R_F.
concepts.example: $30,000 in a 3% term deposit and $70,000 in an equity fund expected to return 9%: w = 0.30 and 0.70, E[R_P] = 0.30 × 3 + 0.70 × 9 = 0.9 + 6.3 = 7.2%.
concepts.contrast: Expected return is linear in the weights; the portfolio standard deviation is not. Weights are proportions of the whole portfolio, not dollar amounts or returns.
concepts.trap: Weights must add to 1 and use market (dollar) values; include the risk-free asset; do not average the returns equally unless the weights are equal. Check that the answer lies between the asset returns.
concepts.mnemonic: Return is a weighted average; weights sum to one.
concepts.formula: w_k = $k/Σ$; Σ w_k = 1; E[R_P] = Σ w_k E[R_k]

concepts.term: Standard deviation of a two-stock portfolio
concepts.definition: σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ_AB w_A σ_A w_B σ_B), where ρ_AB is the correlation of the two stocks' returns. With a risk-free asset (σ = 0, ρ = 0) it reduces to σ = w_P σ_P.
concepts.explain: Portfolio risk is not a weighted average of the two risks: it includes a cross term that depends on how the stocks move together. Compute the two stand-alone terms, add the cross term, and take the square root. The correlation matrix view shows the same three terms.
concepts.example: 60% in A (σ = 20%) and 40% in B (σ = 10%), ρ = 0.3: terms 12² = 144 and 4² = 16, cross term 2 × 0.3 × 12 × 4 = 28.8; σ_P² = 188.8 and σ_P = 13.74%, below the weighted average 0.6 × 20 + 0.4 × 10 = 16%.
concepts.contrast: σ_P versus the weighted average of the σ's (equal only if ρ = 1). Covariance (cov = ρσ_Aσ_B) versus correlation ρ: use the version of the formula that matches what is given.
concepts.trap: Do not forget the square root, do not drop the cross term, do not use cov where ρ is required (or vice versa), and keep σ in decimals or percents consistently. If ρ = 1 you may use the weighted average; for ρ < 1 you may not.
concepts.mnemonic: Two squares plus a cross term, then root.
concepts.formula: σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ_AB w_A σ_A w_B σ_B)

concepts.definition: cov(A,B) = Σ p_i (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]) measures how returns move together; the correlation ρ_AB = cov(A,B)/(σ_A σ_B) is the scaled version, always between −1 and +1. (For historical data the covariance divides by N, or N − 1 for a sample.)
concepts.explain: ρ = +1 means the stocks move in perfect lockstep, 0 means no linear relationship (uncorrelated), −1 means perfect opposite movement. Stocks in the same industry or country tend to have high positive ρ; different industries and countries have lower ρ. The correlation is a property of the pair, like E[R] and σ are of each stock.
concepts.contrast: Covariance has units (%²) and no fixed bounds; correlation is unit-free and bounded by ±1. Correlation is not beta (beta divides by the market variance and is not bounded).
concepts.trap: A correlation outside −1 to +1 signals a units mix or an arithmetic slip. Divide cov by σ_Aσ_B, not by one σ or by a variance. In the portfolio formula use ρ with the σ's, or cov alone, but never cov in the ρ slot.
concepts.mnemonic: Correlation is covariance with the units taken out.
concepts.formula: cov(A,B) = Σ p_i (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]); ρ_AB = cov(A,B)/(σ_A σ_B)

concepts.definition: Whenever ρ_AB < 1, a portfolio of A and B has σ_P below the weighted average of σ_A and σ_B (w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B): the diversification benefit. The lower the correlation, the larger the benefit.
concepts.explain: Because stocks do not move in perfect lockstep, their ups and downs partly cancel, so risk falls while expected return stays the weighted average. As the weight moves from all B to all A, the portfolio traces a curve whose bend depends on ρ. Some weights are inefficient (holding only B when adding some A lowers risk). With many stocks the efficient frontier lies to the left of all individual stocks.
concepts.example: Two stocks with σ = 24% each, 50/50, ρ = 0.25: σ_P² = 2 × (0.5 × 24)² + 2 × 0.25 × 12 × 12 = 288 + 72 = 360, so σ_P = 18.97%, well below the weighted average 24%.
concepts.contrast: Diversification benefit (risk falls for the same weighted return) versus expected return (linear, no benefit). ρ = 1 gives no benefit; ρ = −1 can remove all risk.
concepts.trap: The weighted-average shortcut σ_P = w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B is valid only for ρ = 1. 'Do not put all your eggs in one basket' needs ρ < 1: adding a stock perfectly correlated with the rest does not help.
concepts.formula: σ_P < w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B whenever ρ_AB < 1 (equal when ρ_AB = 1)

figure.title: Shape of the feasible set (E[R_P] against σ_P) for ρ = 1, 0, −1
items: ρ = +1: a straight line from A to B; no diversification benefit, σ_P = w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B.
ρ = 0: a curve bowed to the left of the straight line; some mixes have σ_P below both stocks' σ's.
ρ = −1: two straight segments that touch the vertical axis (σ_P = 0) at w_A = σ_B/(σ_A + σ_B); σ_P = |w_Aσ_A − w_Bσ_B|.
Between the lowest-risk mix and the lower-σ stock the curve is inefficient: the same σ is available with a higher E[R].

concepts.definition: As more stocks are added, portfolio σ falls at a decreasing rate and levels off at σ_M, the volatility of the market. Company-specific (diversifiable, non-systematic) risk can be diversified away; market (non-diversifiable, systematic) risk cannot.
concepts.explain: The first few stocks remove most of the specific risk; later ones help less and less, and a very large portfolio ends up behaving like the market. This is why a well-diversified investor is rewarded only for market risk, which leads to beta and the CAPM in the next chapter.
concepts.example: Illustrative numbers: a one-stock portfolio with σ = 45% falls to about 30% with five stocks and about 25% with fifteen, levelling off near the market's σ_M of 20%: the first stocks cut risk most, and the remaining 20% (σ_M) cannot be removed.
concepts.contrast: Diversifiable (company-specific, non-systematic) versus non-diversifiable (market, systematic) risk. Volatility σ measures total risk; β measures only the systematic part.
concepts.trap: The answer to 'what happens to σ as N grows' is: it decreases, but at a decreasing rate, and never below σ_M. 'Decreases at an increasing rate' and 'eliminates all risk' are wrong.
concepts.mnemonic: Falls, but flattens out at the market.

activities.title: Order the steps: σ from states
activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding the standard deviation of a return from states of the economy in the correct order.
items: List each state's probability and return and check the probabilities add to 1
Compute the expected return E[R] = Σ p_i R_i
Subtract E[R] from each state's return to get the deviations
Square each deviation and multiply by the state's probability
Add the weighted squared deviations to get the variance σ²
Take the square root to get σ in percent
activities.explanation: E[R] must come first because every deviation is measured from it. The weighted squared deviations add up to the variance (no N − 1 with probabilities), and the square root turns it into the standard deviation in the units of returns.

formulas.name: Required return build-up
formulas.formula: E[R] = R_F + risk premium (investor's required return = firm's cost of capital)
formulas.when: Building the return investors need for a given risk, or reading a cost of capital as the investor's E[R].
formulas.trap: The premium is the extra over R_F, so R_F must be added back.

formulas.name: Risk premium (excess return)
formulas.when: Any 'risk premium', 'excess return' or 'equity risk premium' question.
formulas.trap: Subtract the average T-bill return over the same years, not the latest rate.

formulas.name: Fisher relationship (real vs nominal)
formulas.when: Converting nominal historical returns to real ones, or the reverse.
formulas.trap: R_nom − R_inf is only an approximation; divide the growth factors.

formulas.name: Expected return from states
formulas.when: Returns are forecast for states of the economy with probabilities.
formulas.trap: Probabilities must add to 1; do not use the equal-weight average unless the states are equally likely.

formulas.name: Variance and standard deviation from states
formulas.when: States with probabilities; for a portfolio use the portfolio's return in each state.
formulas.trap: No N − 1 with probabilities; finish with the square root.

formulas.name: Historical mean and standard deviation
formulas.when: A list of past returns: population when the data are the whole group, sample when they are a sample.
formulas.trap: N versus N − 1 depends on what the question says the data are.

formulas.name: Normal ranges 68/95/99
formulas.when: Ranges of returns for roughly normal returns.
formulas.trap: Centre on the mean and use the right multiple of σ.

formulas.name: z-score and cumulative normal
formulas.when: Probability of a loss or of exceeding a target, using the cumulative normal table on the table sheet.
formulas.trap: Divide by σ (not σ²); for negative z use 1 − N(|z|); for 'between' subtract the two N's.

formulas.name: Portfolio weights
formulas.when: Turning dollar amounts into weights (including the risk-free asset).
formulas.trap: Weights add to 1 and can be negative when borrowing.

formulas.name: Expected portfolio return
formulas.when: Any portfolio of any number of assets.
formulas.trap: It is linear in the weights; the result lies between the asset returns.

formulas.name: Two-stock portfolio standard deviation
formulas.formula: σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ_AB w_A σ_A w_B σ_B)
formulas.when: Risk of a portfolio of two risky assets; with a risk-free asset σ_P = w_P σ_P.
formulas.trap: Do not forget the square root or the cross term, and do not put cov in the ρ slot.

formulas.name: Covariance and correlation
formulas.formula: cov(A,B) = Σ p_i (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]); ρ_AB = cov(A,B)/(σ_A σ_B)
formulas.when: Measuring how two assets move together from states or data.
formulas.trap: ρ must lie between −1 and +1; divide by σ_Aσ_B, not by σ_M².

formulas.name: Diversification benefit condition
formulas.formula: σ_P < w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B whenever ρ_AB < 1; equal when ρ_AB = 1
formulas.when: Deciding whether combining two stocks lowers risk.
formulas.trap: The weighted-average shortcut is valid only for ρ = 1.

questions.stem: From an investor's point of view the expected return E[R] on an investment is the _____; from the borrowing firm's point of view the very same number is its cost of capital.
options: realized holding period return
coupon rate printed on the bond
required rate of return
accounting return on book equity
questions.explanation: Lenders and investors supply the capital and need E[R] as compensation for the risk they take; the borrower must pay that same rate. One rate, two views: it is the investor's required return and the firm's cost of capital. Realized returns and coupon rates are different things.

questions.stem: Investors in listed pipeline companies of similar risk currently require 6.1% per annum. Bow River Pipelines wants to raise money for a new line that has the same risk as those companies. For this financing decision, the 6.1% is Bow River's:
options: internal rate of return on the new line
accounting return on book equity
cost of capital for projects of that risk
dividend payout ratio
questions.explanation: The rate investors demand for a given level of risk is what the borrower must pay to attract capital, so it is the cost of capital for projects of that risk. An IRR is what a specific project earns; it would be compared with the 6.1%, not equal to it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates a required return from a realized return?
options: A required return is what was actually earned last year; a realized return is what investors hope to earn next year.
A required return is always just the risk-free rate; a realized return is the risk-free rate plus a risk premium.
They are the same number measured at different dates, so over any period the two must be equal to each other.
A required return is the forward-looking reward investors need for the risk; a realized return is what was actually earned.
questions.explanation: Required returns look forward and are tied to risk; realized returns are outcomes. A stock can realize 30% or −10% in a year while investors' required return stays near 9%.

questions.stem: Why should two projects of similar risk be discounted at similar rates?
options: Because projects of similar risk must always have identical cash flows in every future year.
Because investors can choose either, so each must offer a similar expected return for its risk.
Because the discount rate is fixed by contract with the firm's lenders for all projects.
Because the NPV of a project does not depend on which discount rate is used.
questions.explanation: All investments of similar risk should offer similar returns (L06 s45). If one offered more for the same risk, investors would bid its price up until the returns converged.

questions.stem: Aspen Foods considers a new snack line. Shareholders of listed snack-food companies with the same risk require 9.5% per annum. Aspen's best estimate of the new line's expected return is 8.2% per annum. What does this tell Aspen?
options: The line is attractive because 8.2% is well above the risk-free rate, so it earns a premium.
8.2% is below the 9.5% required for this risk, so investors could do better elsewhere; reject the line.
The line is attractive because any positive expected return adds value for shareholders.
The 8.2% should replace 9.5% as the firm's cost of capital, since it is the project's own figure.
questions.explanation: A project must earn at least the return investors require for its risk. Beating the risk-free rate is not enough; the benchmark is the 9.5% cost of capital for similar-risk businesses.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT part of the link between investing and financing?
options: The lender's required return is the borrower's cost of financing.
Investments of similar risk should offer similar returns.
A firm may pick any discount rate it likes for a project, whatever its risk.
E[R] is the required rate of return to the investor and the cost of capital to the firm.
questions.explanation: The cost of capital is set by what investors can earn on other investments of the same risk, not by management's preference. Choosing it freely would let a firm accept bad projects by picking a low rate.

questions.stem: Prairie Gate Rail has just paid an annual dividend of $1.90 per share. Dividends are expected to grow at 4% per year indefinitely and the shares sell for $38.00. Investors' required return, which is also the firm's cost of equity, is what percent per annum?

errors.label: Used D0 instead of D1
errors.explain: The dividend was just paid, so next year's dividend is D1 = D0(1 + g) = $1.976.

errors.label: Left out the growth rate
errors.explain: Required return = dividend yield + capital gain yield; the dividend yield alone is only part of it.

errors.label: Subtracted g from the yield
errors.explain: R = D1/P0 + g. The capital gain yield (g) is added to the dividend yield, not subtracted.

questions.explanation: R = D1/P0 + g: the 9.20% that shareholders require is what Prairie Gate Rail must earn on equity-financed projects of this risk, i.e. its cost of equity.

questions.stem: Foothills Brewing's shares carry about average stock-market risk. The T-bill rate is 2.8% per annum and investors require an equity risk premium of 5.9% per annum for average market risk. What return do investors require on Foothills' shares, in % per annum?

errors.label: Used the premium as the whole required return
errors.explain: The premium is only the extra reward for risk; the investor also needs the risk-free return as the base.

errors.label: Used only the risk-free rate
errors.explain: T-bills are risk free. A risky stock must offer the risk-free rate plus a premium.

questions.explanation: Required return = risk-free rate + risk premium. This build-up is the idea behind the cost of capital: base reward for waiting plus extra reward for bearing risk.

questions.stem: The cost of capital is the return a company actually earned on its investments last year.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The cost of capital is the forward-looking return investors require for the risk of the funds they provide. A firm's past earned return is a realized outcome and may be above or below it.

questions.stem: Which expression builds the required return on a risky asset?
options: E[R] = R_F − risk premium
E[R] = risk premium ÷ R_F
E[R] = σ × R_F
E[R] = R_F + risk premium
questions.explanation: The required return is the risk-free return plus compensation for risk: E[R] = R_F + risk premium, so the premium is E[R] − R_F.

questions.stem: Why does a riskier borrower typically have to pay a higher interest rate than a safer one?
options: Because the risk-free rate is higher for risky borrowers.
Because riskier borrowers always earn higher profits, which they share with lenders.
Because risk-averse lenders need compensation for the extra risk the riskier borrower carries.
Because lenders in Canada are required to charge more to firms with a higher standard deviation.
questions.explanation: Investors and lenders are risk averse, so they want compensation for higher risk. That compensation is the extra interest (risk premium) the borrower pays; the risk-free rate is the same for everyone.

questions.stem: An investor says, "I will not buy this stock unless it offers me at least 10% per annum for the risk I am taking." That 10% is the investor's:
options: required rate of return
realized holding period return
standard deviation of returns
dividend payout ratio
questions.explanation: The minimum expected return an investor accepts for a given risk is the required rate of return. It is the same number the firm sees as its cost of capital.

questions.stem: The risk premium on an asset is:
options: the extra expected return over R_F that compensates for risk, E[R] − R_F
the total expected return of the risky asset, including the risk-free part
the standard deviation of the asset's returns, which measures its risk
the expected return on the whole stock market portfolio
questions.explanation: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F, also called the excess return. It measures only the reward above the risk-free rate, not the whole return and not the risk itself.

questions.stem: Chris will move money from a 3% GIC into a stock fund only if the fund's expected return beats 3% by enough to pay him for the extra risk. Chris is:
options: neutral toward risk
risk seeking
risk free
risk averse
questions.explanation: A risk-averse investor wants compensation (a premium) for taking more risk. An investor who is neutral toward risk would need no extra return; a risk-seeking investor would even accept less.

questions.stem: Pat holds a speculative stock whose expected return is below the T-bill rate because she enjoys the gamble. In the professor's classification Pat is:
options: risk averse
neutral toward risk
risk seeking
diversified
questions.explanation: A risk-seeking investor is willing to give up expected return to take on risk, so a lower expected return is acceptable. A risk-averse investor would never accept less than the risk-free rate for more risk.

questions.stem: Which statement best separates risk aversion from risk avoidance?
options: Risk-averse investors refuse to hold any risky asset.
Risk-averse investors require the same return for every level of risk.
Risk-averse investors prefer the asset with the higher standard deviation when expected returns are equal.
Risk-averse investors do take risk, but only when they are compensated for it.
questions.explanation: The professor's point: risk aversion does NOT mean people do not take on risk. It means they want compensation, so riskier assets must offer a risk premium.

questions.stem: Government T-bills currently pay 2.6% per annum and the stock market is expected to return 9.4% per annum. What is the equity risk premium, in % per annum?

errors.label: Reported the market return, not the excess
errors.explain: The premium is the return above the risk-free rate; subtract R_F.

errors.label: Subtracted in the wrong order
errors.explain: A premium for bearing risk is E[R] − R_F, so it is positive when the risky asset is expected to do better.

errors.label: Added the risk-free rate
errors.explain: The premium is a difference, not a sum.

questions.explanation: Equity risk premium = 9.4% − 2.6% = 6.8% per annum: the extra reward investors expect for holding stocks instead of T-bills.

questions.stem: Over five years Okanagan Orchards' shares returned 18%, −7%, 24%, 11% and 9%. Treasury bills averaged 3.9% per annum over the same five years. What was the stock's average historical risk premium, in % per annum?

steps.label: Average risk premium = average return − average T-bill return

errors.label: Did not subtract the T-bill average
errors.explain: That is the stock's average return, not its premium over the risk-free rate.

errors.label: Divided the sum by N − 1 when averaging
errors.explain: The mean divides by N. The N − 1 divisor belongs only in the sample variance.

questions.explanation: The historical premium is the average stock return minus the average T-bill return: 11.0% − 3.9% = 7.1% per annum.

questions.stem: A Canadian equity fund returned 14%, −9% and 22% over three consecutive years. The one-year T-bill returned 3.0%, 3.4% and 4.1% in those same years. What was the fund's average risk premium over the three years, in % per annum?
solution: Average risk premium = 9.00% − 3.50% = 5.50% per annum (same as averaging the three yearly premiums 11.0, −12.4, 17.9)

errors.label: Subtracted only the latest T-bill return
errors.explain: The risk-free benchmark must be the average over the same three years, not the last year's rate.

errors.label: Reported the fund's average return
errors.explain: That ignores the risk-free return the investor could have earned.

questions.explanation: Average the fund returns, average the T-bill returns over the same years, then subtract: 9.00% − 3.50% = 5.50% per annum.

questions.stem: Analysts expect the stock market to return 10.2% per annum and estimate the equity risk premium at 7.1% per annum. What risk-free rate is implied, in % per annum?
solution: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F, so R_F = E[R] − risk premium

errors.label: Added the premium to the market return
errors.explain: Rearranging premium = E[R] − R_F gives R_F = E[R] − premium; adding goes the wrong way.

errors.label: Reported the premium as the risk-free rate
errors.explain: The premium is the excess over R_F; it is not R_F itself.

questions.explanation: Rearranging risk premium = E[R] − R_F: R_F = 10.2% − 7.1% = 3.1% per annum.

questions.stem: Stock Q is expected to return 12.35% per annum and the risk-free rate is 3.15% per annum. What is Stock Q's risk premium?
questions.explanation: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F = 12.35% − 3.15% = 9.20%. Adding the two gives 15.50%; reversing the order gives −9.20%; subtracting 0.0315 from 12.35 (a percent-decimal mix) gives 12.32%.

questions.stem: Over 1926–2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) small-company stocks averaged 16.6% per year, large-company stocks 12.0% and Treasury bills 3.4%. What was the average risk premium on small-company stocks?
questions.explanation: Small-company premium = 16.6% − 3.4% = 13.2%. The 16.6% is the whole return; 8.6% is the large-company premium (12.0 − 3.4); 4.6% is the difference between the two stock classes (16.6 − 12.0), not a premium over T-bills.

questions.stem: Why do risk-averse investors demand a positive risk premium on stocks?
options: Because they could hold the risk-free asset instead, so a risky asset must be expected to pay more.
Because stocks are guaranteed to beat T-bills in every year, so the premium is certain.
Because the government requires issuers to pay a premium over T-bills.
Because the standard deviation of stocks is always lower than that of T-bills.
questions.explanation: The risk premium is compensation: people want to be paid for taking on risk. It is an expected (average) reward, not a guarantee in any single year.

questions.stem: Using six years of data, the average observed risk premium on large-company stocks was −1.51% per annum. Does this show that investors are not risk averse?
options: Yes. A negative average premium proves that investors accept less than the risk-free rate for bearing risk.
Yes. A negative premium means the stock has become risk free relative to Treasury bills.
No. A premium can never be negative by definition, so the six-year data must contain an error.
No. Expected premiums are positive, but realized premiums can be negative when stock returns come in low or T-bill returns come in high.
questions.explanation: Risk aversion is about what investors require ex ante. Ex post, a short sample can easily produce a negative realized premium; this does not change the required premium going forward.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT another name for the risk premium?
options: the risk-free rate
the excess return
the equity risk premium (when the risky asset is the stock market)
the reward for bearing risk
questions.explanation: The risk-free rate R_F is the base that is subtracted. The risk premium E[R] − R_F is also called the excess return.

questions.stem: An investor who is neutral toward risk needs no compensation for it: she would accept the same expected return on a risky asset as on T-bills.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The lecture's three attitudes are averse, neutral and seeking. Being neutral toward risk means no compensation is needed for risk, so only the expected return matters, not the standard deviation.

questions.stem: The risk premium is also called the _____ return.
options: nominal
real
excess
geometric
questions.explanation: The professor uses 'risk premium' and 'excess return' interchangeably: the return above the risk-free rate, E[R] − R_F.

questions.stem: Which ordering of long-run average annual returns (highest first) matches the U.S. record from 1926 to 2016?
options: large-company stocks, small-company stocks, Treasury bills, long-term bonds
long-term bonds, large-company stocks, small-company stocks, Treasury bills
small-company stocks, large-company stocks, long-term bonds, Treasury bills
Treasury bills, long-term bonds, large-company stocks, small-company stocks
questions.explanation: Averages were roughly 16.6% for small stocks, 12.0% for large stocks, 6.0-6.3% for long-term bonds and 3.4% for T-bills: stocks beat bonds beat bills, and small beat large.

questions.stem: Which observation best illustrates the first lesson of capital market history, that risky assets on average earn a risk premium?
options: Large-company stocks averaged about 8.6 percentage points more per year than Treasury bills.
Treasury bills had the highest standard deviation of all asset classes.
Inflation averaged about 3.0% per year over the same 1926-2016 period.
Long-term corporate bonds outperformed small-company stocks.
questions.explanation: A positive average gap between a risky asset (large stocks, 12.0%) and the risk-free asset (T-bills, 3.4%) is the reward for bearing risk. The other options are false or unrelated to the premium.

questions.stem: How do the first and second lessons of capital market history differ?
options: First: the greater the reward, the greater the risk. Second: risky assets earn a premium on average.
First: bonds beat stocks on average. Second: stocks then beat bills in the long run.
First: returns are normally distributed. Second: returns are independent of risk.
First: risky assets earn a premium on average. Second: greater potential reward comes with greater risk.
questions.explanation: The first lesson is about the average reward for bearing risk; the second links the size of that reward to the size of the risk, measured by standard deviation: small stocks (σ about 31.9%) paid most and were most volatile.

questions.stem: Over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) small-company stocks averaged 16.6% per year against 12.0% for large-company stocks. Why doesn't everyone simply buy small-company stocks?
options: Because small-company stocks have a negative risk premium over T-bills.
Because their returns are far more volatile: σ about 31.9% versus 19.9%.
Because small-company stocks have a lower standard deviation than T-bills.
Because large-company stocks have always outperformed them in every year.
questions.explanation: Higher average return comes with higher volatility, the second lesson of history. The extra return is the compensation for that risk.

questions.stem: In a year when Treasury bills returned 7.7% and inflation was 6.2%, what was the real return on Treasury bills, in % per annum? Use the Fisher relationship.

errors.label: Subtracted inflation from the nominal rate
errors.explain: That shortcut ignores that inflation also erodes the return itself; the Fisher relationship divides the growth factors.

errors.label: Divided the factors upside down
errors.explain: Real purchasing-power growth is (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf), nominal over inflation.

questions.explanation: Fisher: (1 + R_real) = (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf) = 1.077/1.062 = 1.0141, so the real return is about 1.41%, a little less than the simple 1.5% difference.

questions.stem: A pension fund wants a real return of 4.0% per annum when inflation is expected to be 2.5% per annum. What nominal return does it need, in % per annum?

errors.label: Added real return and inflation
errors.explain: Adding ignores the cross term: the extra purchasing power must itself be inflated (0.04 × 0.025 = 0.1%).

errors.label: Divided instead of multiplying
errors.explain: To go from real to nominal you multiply the growth factors; dividing goes from nominal to real.

questions.explanation: Fisher: (1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real) = 1.025 × 1.04 = 1.066, so the fund needs 6.60% nominal.

questions.stem: From 1926 to 2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) small-company stocks averaged a nominal 16.6% per year while inflation averaged 3.0% per year. What was the average real return on small-company stocks, in % per annum?

errors.label: Subtracted inflation from the nominal return
errors.explain: The back-of-envelope 13.6% overstates the real return; the Fisher relationship gives 13.20%.

errors.label: Multiplied by the inflation factor
errors.explain: Real returns come from dividing by the inflation factor, not multiplying.

questions.explanation: Real return = 1.166/1.03 − 1 = 13.20%; the textbook's quick estimate 16.6% − 3.0% = 13.6% is only an approximation.

questions.stem: A Canadian equity fund earned a nominal 9.0% in a year when inflation was 2.4%. What was its real return?
questions.explanation: Real return = 1.090/1.024 − 1 = 6.45%. Simple subtraction gives 6.60% (ignores compounding of inflation), multiplying the factors gives 11.62% (that is how you would go from real to nominal), and 2.4 − 9.0 = −6.60% is the wrong order.

questions.stem: Because Treasury bills averaged 3.4% and inflation 3.0% over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the textbook), the average real return on T-bills was only about 0.4% per year.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. T-bills barely kept pace with inflation: 1.034/1.030 − 1 ≈ 0.39%. They had little default risk but still carried inflation risk.

questions.stem: In one year large-company stocks lost 12% while T-bills gained 3%. Does this contradict the first lesson of capital market history?
options: No. The first lesson is about long-run average premiums; in any single year a large loss is still possible.
Yes. If stocks carry a premium they must beat T-bills in every single year, without exception.
Yes. A single losing year is enough to show that stocks carry no premium at all.
No. Stocks that lose in one year are guaranteed to recover the whole loss within the next year.
questions.explanation: Risk premiums are averages. Individual years can be far below T-bills, which is precisely what volatility (standard deviation) measures.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the historical record for 1926-2016 in the textbook?
options: Treasury bills were more volatile than small-company stocks.
Small-company stocks had the highest standard deviation of the asset classes shown.
Treasury bills earned only slightly more than inflation on average.
Large-company stocks earned a positive average premium over Treasury bills.
questions.explanation: Standard deviations: T-bills about 3.1% versus small-company stocks about 31.9%. Higher average returns came with higher volatility, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Treasury bills are usually called risk free. In what sense can they still be risky for an investor?
options: Inflation can exceed their return, so purchasing power can fall even though the nominal return is positive.
They have a high probability of default because governments often fail to repay.
Their prices swing more than stock prices do because of their very long maturity.
They carry the same standard deviation as small-company stocks, about 31.9% per year.
questions.explanation: T-bills have very little default risk and, being short term, little interest rate risk. The remaining risk is inflation risk: a nominal return of 7% is a loss in purchasing power when inflation is 9%.

questions.stem: Which equation links the nominal return, the inflation rate and the real return?
options: R_real = R_nom − R_inf exactly
(1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf) + (1 + R_real)
R_nom = R_real ÷ R_inf
(1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real)
questions.explanation: The Fisher relationship multiplies growth factors. R_nom − R_inf is only a close approximation when rates are small.

questions.stem: In the professor's notation, the expected return of an asset over states of the economy is calculated as:
options: E[R] = (R_1 + … + R_N)/N, the simple average of the state returns
E[R] = Σ p_i (R_i − E[R])², the weighted squared deviations
E[R] = Σ R_i, the sum of the state returns
E[R] = Σ p_i R_i, the probability-weighted average of the state returns
questions.explanation: With forecast states we multiply each state's return by its probability and add. The simple average (1/N) is the historical version, where every past year counts equally.

questions.stem: An analyst assigns a 30% chance to a boom (stock returns 20%), 50% to normal times (8%) and 20% to a recession (−10%). She multiplies each return by its probability and adds the results. Which measure has she computed?
options: the historical arithmetic average return
the expected return E[R]
the geometric average return
the standard deviation of returns
questions.explanation: Probability-weighted state returns give the expected return: 0.30 × 20 + 0.50 × 8 + 0.20 × (−10) = 8.0%. A historical average would use realized past returns, each with weight 1/N.

questions.stem: How does an expected return computed from states differ from a historical average return?
options: Expected return uses realized past returns; a historical average uses forecast probabilities.
Expected return divides by N − 1 while a historical average divides by N, so the first is larger.
They are the same calculation, and the names are used interchangeably in this course.
Expected return weights projected outcomes by forecast probabilities; a historical average weights each year 1/N.
questions.explanation: Projected future returns come with probabilities, so we weight by p_i. Observed past returns are all equally weighted, 1/N each. The N − 1 divisor appears only in a sample variance, never in a mean.

questions.stem: Which statement about an expected return computed from states is NOT true?
options: It always equals the return in the most probable state.
The state probabilities must add to 1.
It can be a number that no single state actually produces.
A state with a higher probability has more influence on it.
questions.explanation: E[R] is an average over the states, so it generally lies between the lowest and highest state returns and need not match any one of them.

questions.stem: Why do we weight each state's return by its probability rather than average the state returns equally?
options: Because states differ in likelihood, a likelier state should count for more in the average.
Because equal weights would always overstate the risk-free rate in the portfolio.
Because using probabilities makes the variance come out smaller than it otherwise would.
Because the formula sheet only allows weights that add up to 100 rather than 1.
questions.explanation: Probability weighting reflects how likely each outcome is. A 10% recession should not move the average as much as a 50% normal year.

questions.stem: From forecast states, Alder Tech's expected return is 8.7%. The possible state returns are 22%, 9% and −12%. What does the 8.7% mean?
options: It is the return the stock is guaranteed to earn each year if the forecast holds.
It is the return in the single most likely of the three states, the normal case.
It is the lowest return the stock can earn in a bad year, a worst-case figure.
It is the probability-weighted average outcome, not a return the stock will actually earn in any state.
questions.explanation: E[R] summarises the centre of the distribution of outcomes. It is the benchmark against which the spread (σ) is measured; it is not a promise.

questions.stem: A stock's three possible states are given probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.2. Multiplying each state's return by its probability and adding the three products gives a valid expected return.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The probabilities add to 0.9, not 1, so they are incomplete or wrong. The probabilities across all states must sum to 1 before E[R] = Σ p_i R_i is valid.

questions.stem: Northgate Mining shares will return 24% if a commodity boom occurs (probability 35%) and −4% if a bust occurs (probability 65%). What is the expected return, in % per annum?

steps.label: Expected return E[R] = Σ p_i R_i

errors.label: Took the simple average of the two returns
errors.explain: Probabilities are not 50/50, so the equal-weight average is wrong.

errors.label: Attached each probability to the wrong state
errors.explain: The 35% belongs with the boom return 24% and the 65% with the bust return −4%.

questions.stem: Cascade Foods has three forecast states: boom (probability 25%, return 26%), normal (55%, 11%) and recession (20%, −14%). What is its expected return, in % per annum?

errors.label: Took the simple average of the three returns
errors.explain: The states are not equally likely; weight by the probabilities 0.25, 0.55 and 0.20.

errors.label: Multiplied percent probabilities by percent returns
errors.explain: Mixing 25 with 26 instead of 0.25 with 26 inflates the answer by a factor of 100.

errors.label: Treated the recession return as positive
errors.explain: The recession return is −14%; keep the sign when multiplying.

questions.explanation: Weighted sum: 6.50 + 6.05 − 2.80 = 9.75% per annum.

questions.stem: Three states of the economy are equally likely. A stock would return 17% in a strong economy, 6% in a moderate one and −8% in a weak one. What is its expected return, in % per annum?

errors.label: Divided the sum by 2
errors.explain: With three equally likely states each carries weight 1/3, so divide by 3.

errors.label: Left out the weak state
errors.explain: Every state, including the loss state, must be in the sum.

questions.explanation: Equal probabilities of 1/3 make this the simple average of the three state returns: (17 + 6 − 8)/3 = 5.0%.

questions.stem: Peace Arch Software faces four states: boom (probability 10%, return 36%), good (40%, 15%), poor (35%, 2%) and bust (15%, −24%). What is its expected return, in % per annum?

errors.label: Took the simple average of the four returns
errors.explain: The four states have different probabilities, so they cannot be weighted equally.

errors.label: Treated the bust return as positive
errors.explain: The bust return is −24%; its contribution is −3.60.

questions.explanation: Four weighted products add to 6.70% per annum. Check the weights first: 0.10 + 0.40 + 0.35 + 0.15 = 1.00.

questions.stem: Lakeshore Hotels has three states. Boom: probability 0.25, return 30%. Normal: probability not given, return 10%. Recession: probability 0.35, return −15%. What is the expected return, in % per annum?
solution: The probabilities must sum to 1, so p(normal) = 1 − 0.25 − 0.35 = 0.40

errors.label: Left out the normal state
errors.explain: The normal state has probability 0.40 and must be included.

errors.label: Used 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 for the normal state
errors.explain: The remaining probability is 1 minus both other probabilities, 0.40.

questions.explanation: Fill in the missing probability first (1 − 0.25 − 0.35 = 0.40), then take the weighted sum: 6.25%.

questions.stem: You hold 60% of your money in Stock A and 40% in Stock B. The economy has two states: boom (probability 0.40), where A returns 18% and B returns 6%, and bust (probability 0.60), where A returns −4% and B returns 12%. What is the portfolio's expected return, in % per annum?

errors.label: Gave the two stocks equal weights
errors.explain: The money is split 60/40, not 50/50.

errors.label: Put 40% in A and 60% in B
errors.explain: Stock A has weight 0.6 and Stock B has weight 0.4.

errors.label: Averaged the two state portfolio returns equally
errors.explain: The boom has probability 0.40 and the bust 0.60; weight accordingly.

questions.explanation: Compute the portfolio return in each state, then weight by the state probabilities; this equals the weighted average of the stocks' expected returns because E[R] is linear.

questions.stem: Maple Ridge Utilities shares return 15% with probability 40% and 5% with probability 60%. T-bills yield 3.2% per annum. What is the expected risk premium on the shares, in % per annum?
solution: Risk premium = E[R] − R_F = 9.0% − 3.2% = 5.80% per annum

errors.label: Reported E[R] as the premium
errors.explain: The premium is measured above the risk-free rate: subtract R_F.

errors.label: Used the equal-weight average return
errors.explain: The states are 40/60, not 50/50.

questions.explanation: First the expected return (9.0%), then subtract the risk-free rate: 5.8% per annum.

questions.stem: Tamarack Energy's expected return is 7.1% per annum. Its three states are boom (probability 0.30, return 25%), normal (0.50, return 5%) and recession (0.20, return unknown). What return does the recession state imply, in % per annum?

errors.label: Did not divide by the state's probability
errors.explain: −2.9 is the contribution 0.20 × R; divide by 0.20 to get R.

errors.label: Lost the sign
errors.explain: The recession return must be negative to pull a 10.0 weighted sum down to 7.1.

questions.explanation: Work backwards: the other two states contribute 10.0 percentage points, so the recession state must contribute −2.9 and, with weight 0.20, equals −14.5%.

questions.stem: Hurley Energy's shares have three states: strong (probability 0.30, return 18%), average (0.50, 8%) and weak (0.20, −10%). What is the expected return?
questions.explanation: E[R] = 0.30 × 18 + 0.50 × 8 + 0.20 × (−10) = 5.4 + 4.0 − 2.0 = 7.40%. The simple average gives 5.33%; swapping the strong and weak probabilities gives 4.60%; leaving out the weak state gives 9.40%.

questions.stem: A stock returns 14% with probability 60% and −9% with probability 40%. What is its expected return?
questions.explanation: E[R] = 0.60 × 14 + 0.40 × (−9) = 8.4 − 3.6 = 4.80%. Swapping the probabilities gives 0.20%; the simple average gives 2.50%; dropping the negative sign gives 12.00%.

questions.stem: For returns R_i in states with probabilities p_i, the variance of an asset's return is:
options: σ² = Σ p_i R_i, the probability-weighted average of the returns
σ² = √(Σ p_i (R_i − E[R])²), the square root of the weighted squared deviations
σ² = Σ (R_i − E[R])² ÷ (N − 1), the sample formula for historical returns
σ² = Σ p_i (R_i − E[R])², the weighted average of squared deviations from E[R]
questions.explanation: Variance is the weighted average of squared deviations from the expected return. Its square root is the standard deviation. With given probabilities we do not divide by N − 1.

questions.stem: Which statistic does the lecture use to measure the volatility risk of a stock's returns?
options: the standard deviation of returns
the expected return
the risk premium
the correlation coefficient
questions.explanation: Risk (volatility) is measured by σ, the standard deviation of returns, and it goes on the horizontal axis of the risk-return diagram. E[R] measures reward, and the correlation relates two assets.

questions.stem: How does the variance of returns differ from the standard deviation?
options: The variance is the square root of the standard deviation, so it is always the smaller number.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it is in percent while the variance is in squared units.
The variance includes the expected return; the standard deviation does not.
The variance is used on the risk-return diagram; the standard deviation is not.
questions.explanation: σ = √σ². We report and plot σ because it is an ordinary percentage. A variance of 0.0225 corresponds to σ = 0.15, or 15%.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a step in computing the standard deviation of returns from states of the economy?
options: Compute the expected return E[R] = Σ p_i R_i.
Square each state's deviation R_i − E[R].
Divide the weighted sum of squared deviations by (N − 1).
Take the square root of the variance.
questions.explanation: With forecast probabilities the weighted sum of squared deviations already is the variance; there is no N − 1 divisor. N − 1 belongs to the sample variance of historical returns.

questions.stem: Why do we square the deviations (R_i − E[R]) before weighting them?
options: Weighted deviations from E[R] add to zero because they cancel; squaring makes every deviation count as spread.
Because squaring converts percentage deviations into dollar amounts that can be priced.
Because the formula sheet requires every number in a sum to be positive before adding.
Because squaring removes the effect of the probabilities so that all states count equally.
questions.explanation: Without squaring, Σ p_i (R_i − E[R]) = 0 always, so it could not measure risk. Squaring avoids the cancellation and penalises large deviations more.

questions.stem: Stock X and Stock Y both have an expected return of 9%. Stock X has σ = 8% and Stock Y has σ = 24%. What does this tell you?
options: Y is the better stock because a larger σ means a larger return, as the premium is always paid.
X and Y are equally risky because their expected returns are equal, so σ must be equal as well.
X must be a risk-free asset because its σ is lower than Y's, even though σ is not zero.
Y is riskier: its returns spread much more widely around the same expected return, so X is preferred.
questions.explanation: At equal expected returns, the stock with the smaller standard deviation dominates. A larger σ means more uncertainty, not a higher expected return.

questions.stem: You can play one of three fair-coin games, each with a payoff of $1.00 on average: (a) win $1 on heads and $1 on tails; (b) win $0 on heads and $2 on tails; (c) lose $100 on heads and win $102 on tails. Which statement is correct?
options: All three are worth the same to a risk-averse player because the expected payoffs are equal.
Game (c) is worth the most to a risk-averse player because it has the largest possible payoff.
(a) is worth most to a risk-averse player: same $1 mean, but σ of $0, $1 and $101 for (a), (b) and (c).
Game (b) is worth the most to a risk-averse player because it has the lowest standard deviation.
questions.explanation: Expected payoff is $1 in all three, so the difference is risk. For (c) the deviations are ±$101, so σ = $101. A risk-averse player wants compensation for σ, so the riskless game is worth the most.

Using 20 randomly chosen TSX stocks to estimate the volatility of all TSX stocks

the population standard deviation, dividing by N
the probability-weighted formula Σ p_i (R_i − E[R])²
the geometric average of the five returns
questions.explanation: Five years are only a sample of the stock's possible returns, so use the sample formula. The probability-weighted formula is for forecast states with given probabilities.

questions.stem: How do the population and sample standard deviations of the same set of returns differ?
options: The sample version divides by N and the population version by N − 1, so the population version is larger.
They are always exactly equal once N is greater than 30, so the choice never matters.
The sample version divides by N − 1 instead of N, so it is slightly larger; use it when the data are a sample.
The population version squares the deviations, whereas the sample version uses absolute values instead.
questions.explanation: Same numerator (sum of squared deviations); different divisor. Dividing by the smaller number N − 1 gives the larger σ. The difference shrinks as N grows.

questions.stem: Why does the sample standard deviation divide by N − 1 rather than N?
options: Because the first year of data is always discarded as a start-up observation.
Because dividing by N − 1 makes the answer come out as an exact whole-number percentage.
Because N years of prices give only N − 1 holding periods for which returns are measured.
Because the deviations around the sample's own mean are a little too small; dividing by N − 1 corrects that.
questions.explanation: Deviations measured from the sample's own mean are on average too small, so dividing by N would understate the variance. Using N − 1 adjusts for this.

questions.stem: Which statement about a historical standard deviation is NOT correct?
options: Dividing by N − 1 instead of N gives a smaller standard deviation.
The deviations from the mean always sum to zero.
It is measured in the same units as the returns.
A wider spread of returns around the mean gives a larger value.
questions.explanation: Dividing by N − 1 (the smaller number) makes the variance and standard deviation larger, not smaller.

questions.stem: Over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) large-company stocks had an average return of 12.0% and σ = 19.9%; Treasury bills averaged 3.4% with σ = 3.1%. What does this show?

Stocks paid more on average but were far more volatile; T-bill returns stayed close to their average.
Treasury bills were riskier than stocks because their average return was lower.
The two asset classes had the same risk because both averages were positive.
questions.explanation: σ measures how far returns typically fall from their average. 19.9% versus 3.1% shows far greater volatility for stocks, the price of their higher average return.

options: its mean and its skewness
its mean and its standard deviation
its minimum and maximum
its median and its range
questions.explanation: That is why the normal is so convenient: once you know μ and σ there is nothing else to know. All the probability ranges (68%, 95%, 99%) follow from these two numbers.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution, approximately what share of outcomes lies within two standard deviations of the mean?

about 99%

about 95%
questions.explanation: The rule of thumb is 68% within one σ, 95% within two σ and 99% within three σ.

options: Within one σ lies about 68%; below the mean minus one σ lies about 32%.

Within one σ lies about 68% of outcomes; below the mean minus one σ lies only about 16%.
Within one σ lies about 95%; below the mean minus one σ lies about 5%.
questions.explanation: About 32% lies outside ±1σ, split equally between the two tails, so about 16% lies below μ − σ.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a property of the normal distribution?
options: It is bell-shaped and symmetric around its mean.
It is skewed, with the mean above the median.
It is completely described by its mean and standard deviation.
About 68% of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
questions.explanation: The normal is symmetric, so its mean and median coincide; there is no skew.

questions.stem: Why can the normal distribution be used to describe yearly stock returns?
options: Because stock returns are exactly normal in every sample that has been observed.
Because the normal distribution guarantees that no loss ever exceeds three standard deviations.
Because historical returns are roughly mound-shaped and symmetric, and a normal is fully described by μ and σ.
Because the normal distribution removes the need to estimate σ or the mean from data.
questions.explanation: The normal is an approximation, not an exact description: actual distributions are at least roughly mound-shaped and symmetric, which is good enough for the 68/95/99 rules.

questions.stem: U.S. large-company stocks averaged 12.0% with σ = 19.9% over 1926-2016. Treating returns as normal, what does the range −7.9% to 31.9% (12.0% ± 19.9%) tell an investor?

questions.explanation: ±1σ covers about 68% (roughly 2/3) of outcomes. About 1/3 of years fall outside, split between above 31.9% and below −7.9% (about 16% each).
