Horizontal axis: beta. Vertical axis: the expected return E[R].
Horizontal axis: time. Vertical axis: the share price.
questions.explanation: σ is on the x-axis and E[R] on the y-axis. Putting beta on the x-axis gives a different graph, the security market line, which belongs to the next chapter.

questions.stem: Each dot on a risk-return diagram is one stock plotted at its expected return E[R] on the vertical axis and its _____ on the horizontal axis.
options: beta
correlation with the market
standard deviation
dividend yield
questions.explanation: The horizontal axis measures risk as volatility of returns, i.e. the standard deviation σ.

questions.stem: Three stocks plot at (σ, E[R]): Tamarack (14%, 8%), Birchmount (14%, 11%) and Quill (10%, 8%). Which statement is correct?
options: Tamarack dominates both Birchmount and Quill.
Birchmount dominates Quill because it has the higher expected return.
No stock dominates any other.
Birchmount and Quill each dominate Tamarack, but neither dominates the other.
questions.explanation: Birchmount offers a higher return for the same risk (14%); Quill offers the same return for lower risk (10%). Birchmount versus Quill is a trade-off: more return but more risk, so no domination.

questions.stem: How does domination differ from the efficient frontier?
options: Domination compares two points; the efficient frontier is the set of points that no other point dominates.
Domination applies only to bonds; the efficient frontier applies only to stocks.
The efficient frontier is the straight line through the risk-free asset; domination has no line.
They are the same idea described with different words, so no distinction is needed.
questions.explanation: A single stock either is or is not dominated by another. Collecting all stocks that nothing dominates gives the upper-left boundary of the cloud, the efficient frontier.

questions.stem: Which statement about the risk-return diagram is NOT correct?
options: Each dot shows one stock's expected return and standard deviation.
A stock directly above another has the same risk but a higher expected return.
Anywhere other than the efficient frontier a point can be dominated.
A stock plotted up and to the left of another has a higher σ and a lower E[R].
questions.explanation: Up means higher E[R] and left means lower σ, which is better on both counts: that is how one stock dominates another.

questions.stem: Why can an investor ignore a stock that is not on the efficient frontier?
options: Because another point offers more return for the same risk or less risk for the same return.
Because stocks that are off the frontier all have negative expected returns.
Because stocks that are off the frontier have no risk, so they add nothing.
Because the frontier is the only place where the risk-free asset can be found.
questions.explanation: Points not on the frontier can be beaten on return, risk or both, so a rational investor would never choose them in preference to the dominating alternative.

questions.stem: Stock A plots at (σ = 10%, E[R] = 6%) and Stock B at (σ = 20%, E[R] = 12%). What does the diagram tell you?
options: B dominates A because it has the higher expected return, which outweighs the extra risk.
Neither dominates: B has more return but more risk, so the choice depends on risk preference.
A dominates B because it has the lower standard deviation, which outweighs the lower return.
A and B must be perfectly correlated, because both lie on one straight line from the origin.
questions.explanation: Domination needs one stock to be better on return without being worse on risk (or vice versa). Here the two points trade off return against risk, so both can lie on the efficient frontier.

questions.stem: Five stocks plot at (σ, E[R]): P (8%, 5%), Q (12%, 9%), R (12%, 7%), S (18%, 9%) and T (18%, 12%). Which stocks are NOT dominated by any other stock in the list?
options: P, Q and T
P, Q, R and T
Q and T only
P, Q, S and T
questions.explanation: R is dominated by Q (same σ, higher E[R]); S is dominated by Q (same E[R], lower σ). No other stock in the list has both a return at least as high and a σ at least as low as P, Q or T, so they form the upper-left boundary.

questions.stem: A stock with a higher expected return and a lower standard deviation than another stock dominates it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. That is the definition of domination on the risk-return diagram: higher return for lower risk, or the same return for lower risk, or higher return for the same risk.

questions.stem: How are the points for individual stocks on the diagram estimated in the lecture?
options: By computing E[R] and σ from historical returns over a period such as five years.
By reading each stock's beta from a regression of its returns on the market.
By using only the stock's closing price today, with no return history.
By assuming that every stock has the same σ as the market portfolio itself.
questions.explanation: The lecture computes E[R] and σ for each stock over the historical period (e.g. five years) and plots them, with the warning that past performance does not guarantee future returns.

questions.stem: Stocks M and N each have a 50% chance of a boom and a 50% chance of a bust. M returns 18% in the boom and 6% in the bust; N returns 30% in the boom and −6% in the bust. Which statement is correct?
options: N dominates M because its best-case return is higher.
Both have E[R] = 12%, but σ_M = 6% and σ_N = 18%, so M dominates N.
Neither dominates: N has the higher σ, but M has the lower E[R].
M and N plot at the same point on the diagram.
questions.explanation: E[R_M] = 0.5 × 18 + 0.5 × 6 = 12%; E[R_N] = 0.5 × 30 + 0.5 × (−6) = 12%. σ_M = 6% (both outcomes 6 points from the mean) and σ_N = 18%. Same return, lower risk: M dominates N.

questions.stem: Stock V returns 20%, 10% and −5% in states with probabilities 0.30, 0.50 and 0.20. Stock W returns 14%, 9% and 4% in the same states. Which statement is correct?
options: V dominates W because its expected return of 10.0% is greater than W's 9.5%.
W dominates V because W has the lower σ of 3.50% against V's 8.66%.
Neither dominates: V has higher E[R] (10.0% vs 9.5%) but higher σ (8.66% vs 3.50%).
V and W have the same σ of 8.66%, so only expected returns differ.

questions.stem: Where are the best individual stocks on the risk-return diagram?
options: On the upper-left boundary of the cloud of stocks, where no other stock dominates.
At the bottom of the cloud, where expected returns are lowest.
On the lower-right edge where σ is highest and E[R] is lowest.
Only on the vertical axis, at the risk-free rate with σ equal to zero.
questions.explanation: The efficient frontier (the 'red curve' in the lecture) is the set of non-dominated points. Anywhere else can be dominated.

questions.stem: Where would a Treasury bill (the risk-free asset) plot on the risk-return diagram?
options: On the horizontal axis, at the market portfolio's σ and E[R] = 0.
At the origin, where both σ and E[R] are equal to zero.
On the vertical axis, at σ = 0 and a height of R_F.
At the same point as the market portfolio, with the same σ and E[R].
questions.explanation: The risk-free asset has return R_F with zero volatility, so its σ is 0 and its E[R] is R_F: it sits on the vertical axis.

questions.stem: In the professor's notation, the weight w_k of an asset in a portfolio is:
options: the dollar amount invested in that asset divided by the total value of the portfolio
the asset's expected return divided by the portfolio's expected return
the asset's standard deviation divided by the portfolio's standard deviation
the number of shares held in the asset divided by the number of assets in the portfolio
questions.explanation: A weight is a share of dollars: w_k = $k / total portfolio value, so the weights always sum to 1 (100%) because all of the money is invested somewhere (cash counts as an asset). The other options divide returns, risks or share counts, none of which describe how the money is split.

questions.stem: Laurel Ridge Capital holds $18,000 of Prairie Bank shares and $12,000 of Foothills Pipeline shares. Beside the two holdings the analyst writes 0.60 and 0.40. These numbers are called:
options: portfolio weights
expected returns
correlation coefficients
betas
questions.explanation: $18,000 / $30,000 = 0.60 and $12,000 / $30,000 = 0.40: each is the share of total portfolio value held in that stock, which is a portfolio weight. They sum to 1. Expected returns, correlations and betas are properties of the stocks, not of how much money you put in each.

questions.stem: Which expression gives the expected return of a two-stock portfolio with weights w_A and w_B?
options: E[R_P] = √(w_A² E[R_A]² + w_B² E[R_B]² + 2ρ_AB w_A E[R_A] w_B E[R_B])
E[R_P] = w_A E[R_A] + w_B E[R_B]
E[R_P] = w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B
E[R_P] = (E[R_A] + E[R_B]) / 2 whatever the weights
questions.explanation: The portfolio's expected return is the dollar-weighted sum of the expected returns, E[R_P] = Σ w_k E[R_k]. The square-root expression is the shape of the σ_P formula (wrongly applied to returns), and the simple average ignores how the money is actually split.

questions.stem: Consider two statements about a two-stock portfolio. (i) E[R_P] is the weighted average of the two stocks' expected returns. (ii) σ_P is the weighted average of the two stocks' standard deviations. Which is correct?
options: Both are always true
(ii) is always true; (i) is true only when ρ_AB = 1
Neither is ever true
(i) is always true; (ii) is true only when ρ_AB = 1
questions.explanation: Return is linear in the weights, so (i) holds for any correlation. Risk is not linear: σ_P = w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B only in the special case ρ_AB = 1 (and when a weight is zero); for ρ_AB < 1 the portfolio σ is below the weighted average.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the expected return of a long-only two-stock portfolio?
options: It is linear in the portfolio weights
It lies between the expected returns of the two stocks
It depends on the correlation between the two stocks
It can be computed by weighting each stock's expected return by its share of the dollars invested
questions.explanation: E[R_P] = w_A E[R_A] + w_B E[R_B] contains no correlation term: correlation affects the risk of the portfolio, not its expected return. The other three statements are all true of a weighted average with non-negative weights summing to 1.

questions.stem: Why does the correlation between two stocks not appear in the formula for a portfolio's expected return?
options: Correlation only matters for stocks listed in different countries
E[R_P] is a weighted sum of the expected returns, so it is linear
Expected returns of the two stocks are always equal
The weights are always assumed to be equal
questions.explanation: Expectation is linear, so E[w_A R_A + w_B R_B] = w_A E[R_A] + w_B E[R_B] regardless of how R_A and R_B move together. Correlation matters for the variance, where the cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B appears.

questions.stem: A long-only investor mixes Stock A (E[R] = 6%) and Stock B (E[R] = 12%) and reports a portfolio expected return of 13.5%. What does this figure tell you?
options: There is an error: a long-only mix of A and B must have an expected return between 6% and 12%
Diversification has added a bonus return of 1.5% on top of the best stock
It is plausible if the correlation between A and B is very high
It is plausible if the correlation between A and B is negative
questions.explanation: A weighted average with non-negative weights summing to 1 cannot exceed the highest input, here 12%. Diversification lowers risk, not expected return, and correlation does not enter E[R_P] at all. The likely culprit is weights that sum to more than 1 (for example 0.25 and 1.00).

questions.stem: The expected return of a portfolio is the _____ average of the expected returns of its assets, using the portfolio weights.
options: simple
weighted
geometric
variance-weighted
questions.explanation: E[R_P] = Σ w_k E[R_k] is a weighted (arithmetic) average: bigger holdings count for more. A simple average is the special case of equal weights; a geometric average is for compounding past returns (Chapter 8), not for combining assets.

questions.stem: A long-only portfolio of two stocks can have an expected return above that of either stock if the correlation between them is sufficiently negative.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. E[R_P] is a weighted average, so with non-negative weights it must lie between the two expected returns; correlation never enters it. A very negative correlation lowers the portfolio's standard deviation, not its expected return.

questions.stem: You know the dollar holdings and the expected return of each of two stocks. Which sequence gives the portfolio's expected return?
options: Add the two expected returns and divide by two, ignoring the dollar amounts
Multiply each dollar amount by its expected return, add, and divide by the number of stocks
Find the weights, multiply the two weights together, and apply the product to the larger expected return
Find total value; divide each holding by it to get weights; multiply each weight by its expected return; add the products
questions.explanation: Weights come first (dollars / total), then each weight multiplies its own E[R], then the products are added. Averaging the returns while ignoring dollars is the equal-weights shortcut; dividing dollars-times-return by the number of stocks (instead of by total dollars) gives a number in dollars, not a return.

questions.stem: Trillium Fund puts 70% of its money in a Canadian bond index fund (E[R] = 4.5%) and 30% in a global equity fund (E[R] = 10.0%). What is its portfolio expected return?
questions.explanation: E[R_P] = 0.70 × 4.5% + 0.30 × 10.0% = 3.15% + 3.00% = 6.15%. The 8.35% result swaps the weights, 7.25% is the simple average (equal weights assumed) and 13.15% leaves the equity fund unweighted so the weights add to more than 1.

questions.stem: You own 400 shares of Bow Valley Utilities at $36.50 and 250 shares of Rideau Tech at $52.00. Their expected returns are 6.4% and 13.2%. What is the portfolio's expected return?
questions.explanation: Values: 400 × $36.50 = $14,600 and 250 × $52.00 = $13,000, total $27,600, so w = 0.5290 and 0.4710. E[R_P] = 0.5290 × 6.4% + 0.4710 × 13.2% = 9.60%. Using share counts (400 and 250) as the basis for weights gives 9.02%, swapping the weights 10.0%, and the simple average 9.80%.

questions.stem: A cautious investor wants a portfolio expected return of 8% using a GIC fund (E[R] = 4%) and an equity fund (E[R] = 10%). What weight in the equity fund achieves this?
questions.explanation: Set 8 = w × 10 + (1 − w) × 4, so w = (8 − 4)/(10 − 4) = 66.67%. Dividing the target by the equity return (80%) ignores that part of the money earns 4%; 50% is the equal-weight guess; 33.33% is the weight in the GIC fund (the swapped answer).

questions.stem: You have $100,000 to invest. You invest $40,000 in a bank term deposit that is paying interest of 4% per annum, and $60,000 in a well-diversified portfolio of stocks that you think will return 9% per annum. What is your expected return?

errors.label: Averaged the two returns ignoring the dollars
errors.explain: The money is split 40/60, not 50/50; the simple average is only right for equal weights.

errors.label: Swapped the weights
errors.explain: The 60% weight belongs to the 9% stock portfolio, not the 4% deposit.

errors.label: Used weights of 1 on both assets
errors.explain: Weights must sum to 1; adding the two returns uses weights that sum to 2.

questions.explanation: E[R_P] = 0.40 × 4% + 0.60 × 9% = 7.0% per annum (the keyed answer on the sample exam). The result lies between the two returns, closer to 9% because 60% of the money is in stocks. The 6.5% answer is the simple average, the tempting error.

questions.stem: Maple Heights Pension holds 2,400 units of Fund P priced at $18.75 and 1,800 units of Fund Q priced at $31.50. The expected returns are 7.8% for P and 11.4% for Q. What is the portfolio's expected return (% per annum)?

errors.label: Weighted by unit counts instead of dollar values
errors.explain: Weights are shares of dollars invested, not of units held; the two funds have different prices.

errors.label: Swapped the weights
errors.explain: Fund Q is the larger holding, so its (higher) return gets the larger weight.

errors.label: Simple average of the two returns
errors.explain: The holdings are not equal in value, so a simple average misstates the portfolio return.

questions.explanation: Weights come from dollar values (units × price), not unit counts: w_P = 45,000/101,700 = 0.4425. E[R_P] = 0.4425 × 7.8% + 0.5575 × 11.4% = 9.81%, above the simple average of 9.6% because the higher-return fund is the larger holding.

questions.stem: Pinecrest Savings Club allocates 25% of its money to a money-market fund (E[R] = 3.2%), 40% to Canadian equities (E[R] = 9.6%) and 35% to US equities (E[R] = 11.8%). What is the portfolio's expected return (% per annum)?

errors.label: Equal weights of 1/3 on each fund
errors.explain: The weights are 25/40/35, not equal.

errors.label: Attached the weights in the wrong order
errors.explain: Each weight must be paired with its own fund's return; here the 35% belongs to US equities.

errors.label: Used 45% instead of 35% on US equities (weights sum to 1.10)
errors.explain: Always confirm the weights sum to 1 before multiplying.

questions.explanation: E[R_P] = 0.25(3.2) + 0.40(9.6) + 0.35(11.8) = 8.77%. The formula extends to any number of assets: Σ w_k E[R_k] with Σ w_k = 1.

questions.stem: You have $25,000 to invest in Stock X (E[R] = 8.2%) and Stock Y (E[R] = 12.6%) and want a portfolio expected return of 9.8%. How many dollars should you put in Stock Y?

errors.label: Reported the dollars in X instead
errors.explain: That is the amount in X; the question asks for Y.

errors.label: Divided the target by Y's return
errors.explain: That treats the rest of the money as earning 0%, but X earns 8.2%.

errors.label: Forgot the 8.2% earned on the rest: used (9.8 − 8.2)/12.6
errors.explain: Solving w × 12.6 + (1 − w) × 8.2 = 9.8 gives a denominator of 12.6 − 8.2, not 12.6.

questions.explanation: Because the weights sum to 1, w_Y = (target − E[R_X]) / (E[R_Y] − E[R_X]) = 0.3636, so $9,090.91 goes in Y and $15,909.09 in X. Check: 0.6364 × 8.2% + 0.3636 × 12.6% = 9.8%.

questions.stem: A portfolio is 60% Stock A and 40% Stock B. Boom (probability 0.30): A returns 24%, B returns 4%. Normal (0.50): A 10%, B 6%. Recession (0.20): A −12%, B 12%. What is the portfolio's expected return (% per annum)?
solution: Portfolio return in each state = 0.6 R_A + 0.4 R_B: Boom 14.4 + 1.6 = 16.0%; Normal 6.0 + 2.4 = 8.4%; Recession −7.2 + 4.8 = −2.4%

errors.label: Averaged the three state returns with equal weight
errors.explain: The states are not equally likely; each state's return must be multiplied by its probability.

errors.label: Used 40% in A and 60% in B
errors.explain: A is 60% of the money, B is 40%.

errors.label: Left out the recession state (probabilities add to 0.80)
errors.explain: Probabilities must sum to 1: the recession state (probability 0.20) cannot be dropped.

questions.explanation: Compute the portfolio return state by state, then take the probability-weighted average: 8.52%. Linearity means the same answer comes from weighting the stocks' own expected returns (9.8% and 6.6%).

questions.stem: You invest your own $50,000 plus $20,000 borrowed at the risk-free rate of 3.5% per annum, all in an index fund with an expected return of 9.5%. What is the expected return on your own $50,000 (% per annum)?
solution: Your own money is the base: w_fund = 70,000 / 50,000 = 1.40 and w_F = −20,000 / 50,000 = −0.40 (borrowing is a negative weight); 1.40 − 0.40 = 1

errors.label: Ignored the borrowing cost
errors.explain: The loan costs 3.5% on 40% of your capital; it must enter with a negative weight.

errors.label: Gave the loan a positive weight of +0.40
errors.explain: Borrowing is a negative position in the risk-free asset; weights then sum to 1.00, not 1.80.

errors.label: Reported the fund's own return
errors.explain: Borrowing magnifies the expected return on your own money: you earn 9.5% on $70,000 but pay interest on $20,000.

questions.explanation: With borrowing, weights are measured against your own money: 1.40 in the fund and −0.40 in the risk-free asset (still summing to 1). E[R_P] = 1.40(9.5) − 0.40(3.5) = 11.9%, higher than 9.5% because leverage adds expected return (and risk).

questions.stem: A portfolio's weights are +1.25 in an equity index fund and −0.25 in the risk-free asset. What does the negative weight mean?
options: The investor has invested in an asset with a negative expected return
The weights are invalid because portfolio weights must lie between 0 and 1
The investor has borrowed at the risk-free rate and invested more than 100% of her own money in the fund
The investor holds fewer dollars in the fund than in the risk-free asset
questions.explanation: Weights must sum to 1 (1.25 − 0.25 = 1) but individual weights can be negative: a negative risk-free weight is borrowing, and the borrowed money lets her hold 125% of her own money in the fund. This is the w_F < 0, w_P > 1 end of the capital allocation line.

questions.stem: You hold $30,000 of Stock A (E[R] = 5%) and $20,000 of Stock B (E[R] = 11%). What is the portfolio's expected return?
options: None of the above
questions.explanation: w_A = 30,000/50,000 = 0.60 and w_B = 0.40, so E[R_P] = 0.60 × 5% + 0.40 × 11% = 3.0% + 4.4% = 7.40%, which is not listed. 8.00% is the simple average of 5% and 11%, 8.60% swaps the weights (0.4 × 5% + 0.6 × 11%), and 16.00% adds the returns (weights of 1 on both).

questions.stem: Which expression gives the standard deviation of a two-stock portfolio in terms of the weights, the standard deviations and the correlation?
options: σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ_AB w_A σ_A w_B σ_B)
σ_P = w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ_AB w_A σ_A w_B σ_B
σ_P = w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B
σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B²)
questions.explanation: The formula adds the two weighted variances and the correlation cross-term, then takes the square root. Without the square root the result is a variance; w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B is right only when ρ_AB = 1; dropping the cross-term assumes ρ_AB = 0.

questions.stem: An analyst evaluates √(0.5² × 20² + 0.5² × 30² + 2 × 0.4 × 0.5 × 20 × 0.5 × 30) and gets 21.1 (in percent). Which quantity has she computed?
options: The expected return of a 50/50 portfolio of the two stocks
The standard deviation of a 50/50 portfolio of the two stocks
The covariance between the two stocks
The beta of the portfolio against the market
questions.explanation: The expression has the exact shape of σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B) with w = 0.5, σ = 20% and 30%, ρ = 0.4. Expected return would be a plain weighted sum, covariance has no weights, and beta needs the market's variance.

questions.stem: A text gives the portfolio SD formula with ρ_AB in the cross-term; a case study gives cov(A,B) instead. Which statement about the two forms is correct?
options: With a covariance you still write 2 ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B, putting the covariance in the ρ slot
The covariance form has no cross-term because covariance already includes the weights
They are the same formula because cov(A,B) = ρ_AB σ_A σ_B: use 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B) when the covariance is given
The covariance form applies only when ρ_AB = 0
questions.explanation: Since cov(A,B) = ρ_AB σ_A σ_B, the cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B equals 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B). Putting a covariance (for example 0.021) where a correlation belongs is the classic cov-as-ρ error and nearly deletes the cross-term.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT needed to compute the standard deviation of a two-stock portfolio?
options: The expected returns of the two stocks
The portfolio weights
The standard deviation of each stock
The correlation (or covariance) between the two stocks
questions.explanation: σ_P depends on weights, individual risks and the correlation or covariance. Expected returns affect E[R_P] but never enter the risk formula.

questions.stem: Why is the standard deviation of a two-stock portfolio normally smaller than w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B?
options: Because variances are added after weighting, which always makes the total smaller
Because the portfolio's expected return is a weighted average
Because the weights are squared in the formula, and squares are always smaller
Because the stocks do not move in lockstep, so one's bad outcome is partly offset by the other's
questions.explanation: The weighted average of SDs is exactly what the formula gives at ρ = 1, where the cross-term is as large as it can be. For ρ < 1 the cross-term shrinks, so σ_P falls below the weighted average. Squared weights alone do not explain the gap: at ρ = 1 they still give the weighted average.

questions.stem: A 50/50 mix of Stock A (σ = 24%) and Stock B (σ = 12%) is reported to have σ_P = 18%. What does this tell you about the correlation?
options: ρ_AB = 0, because the stocks are independent
ρ_AB = −1, because the risks offset each other
ρ_AB = +1, because 18% equals the weighted average 0.5 × 24% + 0.5 × 12%
Nothing: σ_P always equals the weighted average of the two SDs
questions.explanation: The weighted average of the SDs is 0.5(24) + 0.5(12) = 18%. σ_P reaches that ceiling only when the returns are perfectly positively correlated, so ρ_AB = +1 and there is no diversification benefit. For ρ = 0 the SD would be 13.4% and for ρ = −1 it would be 6%.

questions.stem: A 40/60 mix of Stock A (σ = 30%) and Stock B (σ = 20%) has a portfolio standard deviation of exactly zero. What must be true?
options: ρ_AB = 0, because the two stocks are independent
ρ_AB = −1, so the weighted risks 0.4 × 30% = 12% and 0.6 × 20% = 12% cancel exactly
ρ_AB = +1, because the weights add up to one
Any correlation produces this result because the weights are well chosen
questions.explanation: With ρ = −1 the formula is a perfect square: σ_P = |w_A σ_A − w_B σ_B| = |12% − 12%| = 0. Only perfect negative correlation allows the risk to cancel completely; at ρ = 0 this mix has σ_P = 16.97%.

questions.stem: The weights and standard deviations of two stocks are held fixed while the correlation between them falls from 0.6 to 0.1. What happens to σ_P?
options: σ_P falls, because the cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B shrinks
σ_P rises, because lower correlation means more uncertainty
σ_P is unchanged, because the weights and σ's are unchanged
σ_P cannot be determined without the expected returns
questions.explanation: ρ appears only in the cross-term, which is proportional to ρ (positive weights). Lowering ρ lowers the variance and therefore σ_P; the expected returns play no role in the risk formula.

questions.stem: A portfolio of 50% in an equity fund with σ = 20% and 50% in Treasury bills has a standard deviation of 10%.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A risk-free asset has σ_F = 0 and no correlation with anything, so the formula collapses to σ_P = w_P σ_P = 0.50 × 20% = 10%. The capital allocation line is straight for this reason.

questions.stem: The variance of a two-stock portfolio equals the weighted average w_A σ_A² + w_B σ_B² of the two stocks' variances.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The weights are squared (w_A² σ_A² + w_B² σ_B²) and a covariance cross-term 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B) is added. Risk is not linear in the weights, unlike expected return.

questions.stem: If the correlation ρ_AB between two stocks is 0, the cross-term in the formula for the portfolio variance _____.
options: doubles
becomes negative
equals w_A w_B
disappears
questions.explanation: The cross-term 2ρ_AB w_A σ_A w_B σ_B is proportional to ρ_AB, so it is zero when ρ_AB = 0 and σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B²). It is negative only when ρ_AB < 0.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly computes the standard deviation of a two-stock portfolio from weights, SDs and a correlation?
options: Find the weights; compute w_A²σ_A² and w_B²σ_B²; add the cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B; sum to get the variance; take the square root
Find the weights; take the square root of each term; then add the terms together
Sum the two squared terms; take the square root; then add the cross-term
Find the weights; multiply the two SDs together; take the square root; weight the result
questions.explanation: The square root is the last step and applies to the whole variance. Taking square roots term by term (or before adding the cross-term) breaks the formula and tends to reproduce a weighted average of SDs.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 20% and Stock B has σ = 30%. Their correlation is 0.3. What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 60% in A and 40% in B?
questions.explanation: Variance terms: 0.6² × 20² = 144.0; 0.4² × 30² = 144.0; cross-term 2(0.3)(0.6)(20)(0.4)(30) = 86.4. Sum = 374.4, so σ_P = √374.4 = 19.35%. The 24.00% answer is the ρ = 1 weighted average, 16.97% omits the correlation cross-term, and 3.74% forgets the square root (a decimal variance of 0.0374).

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 15% and Stock B has σ = 25%; cov(A,B) = 0.0150 (returns in decimals). What is the standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of the two?
questions.explanation: Using the covariance form: variance = 0.5²(0.15²) + 0.5²(0.25²) + 2(0.5)(0.5)(0.0150) = 0.005625 + 0.015625 + 0.0075 = 0.028750, so σ_P = 16.96%. Putting 0.0150 in the ρ slot of the correlation formula gives 14.67%; omitting the covariance gives 14.58%; the weighted average is 20.00% (the ρ = 1 result; here ρ = 0.4).

questions.stem: Two uncorrelated stocks (ρ = 0) have σ = 16% and σ = 28%. What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 70% in the first and 30% in the second?
questions.explanation: With ρ = 0 the cross-term vanishes: variance = 0.7²(16²) + 0.3²(28²) = 125.44 + 70.56 = 196.00, so σ_P = 14.00%. The 19.60% answer is the weighted average (ρ = 1 shortcut), 20.36% forgets to square the weights, and 1.96% stops at the variance.

questions.stem: You hold $12,000 in the Bay Street Equity Fund (σ = 18%) and $8,000 in Treasury bills. What is the standard deviation of the whole portfolio?
questions.explanation: The T-bills are risk-free (σ = 0), so σ_P = w × σ_fund with w = 12,000/20,000 = 0.60: 0.60 × 18% = 10.80%. Using the T-bill weight (7.20%) uses the wrong weight; 18.00% ignores the T-bills; 6.48% squares the weight without squaring σ.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 22% and Stock B has σ = 34%; their correlation is 0.35. What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 60% in A and 40% in B (% per annum)?

steps.label: Variance of the A component, w_A²σ_A²
Variance of the B component, w_B²σ_B²

errors.explain: σ_P is the square root of the portfolio variance; stopping at the variance gives a number in squared units.

errors.label: Used the weighted average of the two SDs (the ρ = 1 shortcut)
errors.explain: w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B is the answer only when ρ = 1; for ρ < 1 the portfolio SD is smaller.

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

questions.explanation: σ_P = √(0.36·22² + 0.16·34² + 2·0.35·0.6·22·0.4·34) = 22.02%. This is below the 26.80% weighted average because ρ = 0.35 < 1 – the diversification benefit – and above the 18.95% you get by wrongly ignoring correlation.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 20% and Stock B has σ = 30%; the covariance of their returns is 0.0210 (returns in decimals). What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 60% in A and 40% in B (% per annum)?
solution: Use cov directly: variance = w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B)

errors.label: Put the covariance in the ρ slot of the correlation formula
errors.explain: Covariance already contains σ_A σ_B; the correlation formula needs ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B) = 0.35, not 0.0210.

errors.label: Forgot the 2 on the cross-term
errors.explain: The cross-term appears twice (A with B and B with A), hence the 2.

errors.label: Dropped the covariance term
errors.explain: A covariance of 0.0210 is positive and adds to the portfolio variance; leaving it out understates the risk.

questions.explanation: With a covariance given, use σ_P² = w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B). Work in decimals throughout (cov = 0.0210 is in decimal squared units) and convert σ_P back to percent at the end: 19.72%.

questions.stem: Stock A (σ = 24%) and Stock B (σ = 18%) are uncorrelated (ρ = 0). What is the standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of the two (% per annum)?

steps.label: Variance of the A component, w_A²σ_A²
Variance of the B component, w_B²σ_B²

solution: ρ = 0, so the cross-term is zero: σ_P² = w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B²

errors.label: Used the weighted average of the SDs
errors.explain: That is the ρ = 1 answer; with ρ = 0 the portfolio SD is lower.

errors.label: Reported the variance as a percent (decimal 0.0225)
errors.explain: 225 is the variance in %²; the SD is its square root.

errors.label: Took √(σ_A² + σ_B²) without weights
errors.explain: Each variance must be multiplied by the square of its weight.

questions.explanation: For uncorrelated stocks σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B²) = √225 = 15.00%, well below the 21.00% weighted average (the ρ = 1 value).

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 25% and Stock B has σ = 15%, and the two are perfectly positively correlated (ρ = +1). What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 40% in A and 60% in B (% per annum)?

steps.label: Weighted risk of A, w_A σ_A
Weighted risk of B, w_B σ_B

solution: With ρ = 1 the formula is a perfect square: σ_P = √(w_Aσ_A + w_Bσ_B)² = w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

errors.label: Reported the variance (361) scaled to a decimal percent
errors.explain: 361 is the variance; the SD is its square root.

errors.label: Added the stand-alone SDs with no weights
errors.explain: Each SD is multiplied by its weight; the weights sum to 1.

questions.explanation: ρ = +1 is the one case where risk is linear: σ_P = 0.4(25) + 0.6(15) = 19.00%. Any ρ < 1 would give less than this, which is why 19% is the upper limit for every mix of these two stocks.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 30% and Stock B has σ = 20%, and the two are perfectly negatively correlated (ρ = −1). What is the standard deviation of a portfolio with 60% in A and 40% in B (% per annum)?

steps.label: Weighted risk of A, w_A σ_A
Weighted risk of B, w_B σ_B

solution: With ρ = −1 the formula is the perfect square (w_Aσ_A − w_Bσ_B)², so σ_P = |w_A σ_A − w_B σ_B|

errors.label: Reported the variance (as a decimal) instead of its square root
errors.explain: σ_P is the square root of the portfolio variance; stopping at the variance gives a number in squared units.

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

errors.label: Used ρ = +1 in the cross-term (added the two risks)
errors.explain: The cross-term is 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B with ρ = −1: it subtracts 288, it does not add it.

questions.explanation: At ρ = −1 the two risks offset: σ_P = |18% − 8%| = 10.00%, far below the 26.00% weighted average. Changing the weights to 40/60 would give 12% − 12% = 0, a riskless portfolio.

questions.stem: Of a $40,000 portfolio, $25,000 is invested in a Canadian equity fund with σ = 19.2% and the rest in Treasury bills. What is the portfolio's standard deviation (% per annum)?
solution: T-bills have σ = 0 and ρ = 0 with the fund, so the formula reduces to σ_P = w_P σ_P

errors.label: Used the T-bill weight (0.375)
errors.explain: The risk comes from the equity fund, so its weight (0.625) multiplies σ.

errors.label: Reported the fund's own SD
errors.explain: Holding part of the money in T-bills scales the risk down in proportion.

errors.label: Squared the weight and σ without a square root (decimal variance)
errors.explain: σ_P = w σ already; no squaring is needed for the risk-free mix.

questions.explanation: With a risk-free asset the cross-term and the risk-free variance both vanish, so σ_P is simply the risky weight times the risky σ: 0.625 × 19.2% = 12.00%. This straight-line scaling is why a capital allocation line is a straight line.

questions.stem: You use $40,000 of your own money and borrow $20,000 at the risk-free rate of 3% per annum, investing all $60,000 in a fund with E[R] = 9% and σ = 14%. What is the standard deviation of the return on your own $40,000 (% per annum)?
solution: Weights on your own money: w_fund = 60,000/40,000 = 1.50 and w_F = −20,000/40,000 = −0.50
σ_P = w_fund × σ_fund (the risk-free asset adds no variance) = 1.50 × 14% = 21.00%

errors.label: Reported the fund's own SD
errors.explain: Borrowing to hold 150% of your capital in the fund multiplies the risk by 1.5.

errors.label: Used the borrowing weight (0.5)
errors.explain: The fund weight is 1.5, not 0.5; the risk-free weight is −0.5.

errors.label: Counted the loan as a positive 0.5 weight: (1.5 + 0.5) × 14
errors.explain: Borrowing is a negative weight; the weights must sum to 1 (1.5 − 0.5), and the risk-free asset adds no risk.

questions.explanation: Leverage scales risk linearly: σ_P = 1.5 × 14% = 21.00%. The loan has no variance (it is risk-free), so all of the risk comes from the 150% position in the fund.

questions.stem: You hold $30,000 of Stock A (σ = 28%) and $20,000 of Stock B (σ = 16%). The correlation between them is 0.2. What is the standard deviation of the portfolio (% per annum)?

errors.label: Reported the variance (as a decimal) instead of its square root
errors.explain: σ_P is the square root of the portfolio variance; stopping at the variance gives a number in squared units.

errors.label: Used the weighted average of the two SDs (the ρ = 1 shortcut)
errors.explain: w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B is the answer only when ρ = 1; for ρ < 1 the portfolio SD is smaller.

errors.label: Left out the correlation cross-term (treated ρ as 0)
errors.explain: The cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B carries the correlation; dropping it assumes the stocks are uncorrelated.

questions.explanation: Convert dollars to weights first (0.60, 0.40), then apply σ_P = √(w_A²σ_A² + w_B²σ_B² + 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B) = 19.14%, below the 23.20% weighted average.

questions.stem: Invest 75% of your funds in Asset X (E[R] = 9%, σ = 14%) and 25% in Asset Y (E[R] = 15%, σ = 20%). The correlation between X and Y is 0.3. What is the standard deviation of the portfolio (% per annum)?
