questions.stem: A portfolio is 50% Stock A and 50% Stock B. Boom (probability 0.25): A 20%, B −4%. Normal (0.50): A 8%, B 6%. Recession (0.25): A −10%, B 14%. What is the standard deviation of the portfolio's return (% per annum)?
solution: Portfolio return in each state: Boom 0.5(20) + 0.5(−4) = 8%; Normal 0.5(8) + 0.5(6) = 7%; Recession 0.5(−10) + 0.5(14) = 2%
σ_P = √5.50 = 2.35% per annum (the formula route gives the same: σ_A = 10.71%, σ_B = 6.38%, cov = −66.75 %² = −0.006675 in decimals, ρ = −0.98)

errors.label: Reported the variance (5.50) instead of its square root
errors.explain: 5.50 is a variance in %²; the SD is its square root.

errors.label: Weighted average of the two stocks' SDs (10.71% and 6.38%)
errors.explain: The two stocks are almost perfectly negatively correlated (ρ ≈ −0.98), so averaging their SDs overstates the risk by a wide margin.

errors.label: Gave the three states equal weight
errors.explain: States have probabilities 0.25/0.50/0.25; equal weighting changes both the mean and the variance.

questions.explanation: When the data are given by state, the quickest route is to compute the portfolio's return in every state and then treat it as a single asset: E[R_P] = 6.00%, σ_P² = 5.50, σ_P = 2.35%. The formula route (σ's, cov, weights) gives the same answer; A and B hedge each other so risk falls from about 8.5% (the weighted average) to 2.35%.

questions.stem: The correlation coefficient ρ_AB between the returns of stocks A and B is:
options: cov(A,B) / σ_B², the slope of A's returns on B's returns
cov(A,B) / (σ_A σ_B), a unit-free number between −1 and +1
cov(A,B) × σ_A × σ_B, a number in squared percent
σ_A σ_B / cov(A,B), which is always above 1
questions.explanation: ρ_AB = cov(A,B)/(σ_A σ_B) standardizes the covariance by the two standard deviations, so it has no units and lies in [−1, +1]. Dividing by one variance gives a regression slope (beta-type measure), not a correlation.

questions.stem: Which pair of stocks is most likely to have the highest correlation of returns?
options: Two Canadian chartered banks
A Calgary oil producer and a Vancouver software company
A Canadian bank and a Japanese automaker
A gold miner and a regulated electric utility
questions.explanation: Stocks in the same industry and the same country respond to the same news (interest rates, regulation, the Canadian economy), so their returns move together and ρ is high and positive. Different industries or different countries have lower correlations, and lower correlation means a bigger diversification benefit.

questions.stem: A scatter plot puts Stock A's yearly returns on the horizontal axis and Stock B's on the vertical axis. The points sit tightly around a straight line sloping downward from left to right. The correlation is closest to:
questions.explanation: A downward-sloping tight cloud means that when A is high B is low: strong negative correlation, near −1. A formless blob is near 0, and an upward-sloping tight line is near +1.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts covariance and correlation?
options: Covariance is bounded by ±1, whereas correlation is measured in squared percent
Covariance and correlation always have opposite signs for the same pair of stocks
Correlation measures the average return of two stocks, covariance measures their risk
Correlation is covariance scaled by σ_A σ_B: unit-free and bounded by ±1, unlike covariance
questions.explanation: Both share the same sign (the sign of the co-movement). Dividing the covariance by σ_A σ_B removes the units and caps the result at ±1 so strengths are comparable across pairs; the raw covariance grows with the stocks' volatility.

questions.stem: Which of the following could NOT be the correlation coefficient between two stocks?
questions.explanation: Correlation is always between −1 and +1, so +1.20 is impossible; it signals an arithmetic or units error, for example mixing percent and decimals.

questions.stem: Why do we divide the covariance by σ_A σ_B to get the correlation?
options: It converts the covariance from percent into dollars
It makes the covariance equal to the portfolio's expected return
It removes the units, so ρ shows only the direction and strength of co-movement
It ensures that the correlation always comes out positive
questions.explanation: A covariance of 0.03 could be strong for two calm stocks or weak for two volatile ones. Dividing by σ_A σ_B standardizes the relationship so that +1, 0 and −1 mean the same thing for every pair.

questions.stem: A student computes cov(A,B), σ_A and σ_B from a five-year sample, but divides all three sums by N = 5 instead of N − 1 = 4. What happens to the correlation?
options: It becomes too high by a factor of 5/4
It is unchanged, because the same factor cancels
It becomes too low by a factor of 4/5
It is no longer bounded by ±1
questions.explanation: Each of cov, σ_A² and σ_B² is a sum divided by N or N − 1. In ρ = cov/(σ_Aσ_B) the denominators are the same factor 1/(N−1) in numerator and in √(σ_A² σ_B²), so it cancels. (Mixing N for one term and N − 1 for another would, however, bias ρ.)

questions.stem: The correlation between two Canadian bank stocks is estimated at 0.85. What does this imply for combining them in a portfolio?
options: Some benefit remains because ρ < 1, but it is small since the stocks move together
There is no diversification benefit at all, since the correlation is positive
The portfolio will be riskless, because stocks that move together offset each other
The portfolio's expected return will be lower than either stock's
questions.explanation: Any ρ below 1 gives some benefit (σ_P lower than the weighted average of the σ's), but at 0.85 the cross-term is almost at its maximum so the gain is modest. The benefit comes at no cost in expected return because E[R_P] is a weighted average.

questions.stem: cov(A,B) = −0.0150. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The two stocks are perfectly negatively correlated
The stocks are uncorrelated because the number is close to zero
One of the stocks must have a negative expected return
The returns tend to move in opposite directions; strength needs ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B)
questions.explanation: The sign shows direction (negative: when A is above its mean B tends to be below its mean). The size depends on the stocks' volatilities, so −0.0150 could be anything from weak to perfect negative correlation until it is converted to ρ.

questions.stem: A student reports a correlation of 1.18 between two stocks. What is the best interpretation?
options: The stocks are more than perfectly correlated, so diversification will increase risk
It is valid if the covariance is large enough
The value is impossible: ρ must lie in [−1, +1], so there is a units or arithmetic error to find
It indicates leveraged stocks with betas above 1
questions.explanation: A correlation outside [−1, +1] is always a mistake: typically a wrong denominator (for example dividing by one variance, or by σ_A σ_B in different units), a unit mix of percent and decimals, or an arithmetic slip. Recheck before using the number.

questions.stem: Every return on Stock A is doubled (a 2× leveraged version, A' = 2A) while Stock B is unchanged. What happens to cov(A',B) and to ρ(A',B) compared with cov(A,B) and ρ(A,B)?
options: Both double
The covariance doubles; the correlation is unchanged
The covariance is unchanged; the correlation doubles
Both are unchanged
questions.explanation: cov(2A, B) = 2 cov(A,B), but σ_(2A) = 2σ_A as well, so ρ = 2cov/(2σ_A σ_B) is unchanged. This is why correlation, not covariance, describes the pattern of co-movement independent of scale.

questions.stem: Returns of two stocks over five years are given. The sample covariance is the sum of products of deviations from the means divided by:
options: The sum of the probabilities
questions.explanation: The professor uses the sample version (÷(N − 1)) for a short history such as five years of one stock, and the population version (÷N) only when the data are the whole population. Probabilities are used instead of a divisor when returns are given by state of the economy.

questions.stem: Returns of two stocks are listed for three states of the economy with probabilities 0.20, 0.50 and 0.30. How is cov(A,B) computed?
options: Σ p_i (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]), with no division by N − 1
Σ (R_A,i − E[R_A])(R_B,i − E[R_B]) / (N − 1) with N = 3
Σ p_i R_A,i R_B,i, without subtracting the means
Σ p_i (R_A,i − R_B,i)², the squared difference between the two stocks' returns
questions.explanation: With probabilities given, each state's deviation product is weighted by its probability: cov = Σ p (R_A − E_A)(R_B − E_B). Dividing by N − 1 is for historical samples; skipping the deviations gives E[R_A R_B], which is not the covariance.

questions.stem: If cov(A,B) = 0, then the correlation between A and B is 0.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B), so a zero numerator gives ρ = 0 (as long as both σ are positive). Uncorrelated stocks have no cross-term in the portfolio variance.

questions.stem: A correlation of −0.9 between two stocks indicates a stronger linear relationship than a correlation of +0.3.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. Strength is the magnitude |ρ| (0.9 versus 0.3); the sign only gives the direction. −0.9 means the stocks move almost exactly opposite to each other, the best case for diversification.

questions.stem: A correlation of 0.5 between A and B means that B's return is always exactly half of A's return.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A correlation of 0.5 describes a loose tendency to move together; it says nothing about a fixed proportion. Only |ρ| = 1 means an exact linear relationship.

questions.stem: Two stocks in the same industry and the same country tend to have a _____ correlation.
options: low positive
negative
high positive
zero
questions.explanation: Common industry and country factors drive both stocks, so their returns rise and fall together; stocks in different industries or countries have lower correlations and offer more diversification.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 24% and Stock B has σ = 15%; cov(A,B) = 0.0180 (decimals). What is the correlation between A and B?
questions.explanation: ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B) = 0.0180/(0.24 × 0.15) = 0.0180/0.0360 = 0.50. Dividing by σ_A² (0.31) or σ_B² (0.80) gives a beta-type slope, and reporting 0.02 simply quotes the covariance as if it were ρ.

questions.stem: In three equally likely states of the economy, Stock X returns 15%, 6% and −3%, and Stock Y returns 4%, 10% and 10%. What is cov(X,Y), with returns as decimals?
questions.explanation: E[R_X] = 6%, E[R_Y] = 8%. Deviation products (decimals): 0.09 × (−0.04) = −0.0036, 0 × 0.02 = 0, (−0.09)(0.02) = −0.0018. With probability 1/3 each, cov = (−0.0036 + 0 − 0.0018)/3 = −0.0018. Dividing by N − 1 gives −0.0027, leaving the sum undivided gives −0.0054, and skipping the means (E[XY]) gives 0.0030.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 18% and Stock B has σ = 30%; their correlation is −0.5. What is cov(A,B), with returns as decimals?
questions.explanation: cov(A,B) = ρ σ_A σ_B = (−0.5)(0.18)(0.30) = −0.0270. The positive 0.0270 loses the sign, −0.0900 omits σ_B, and −0.1200 uses the average of the two σ's in place of their product.

questions.stem: Strong economy (probability 0.30): Stock A returns 18%, Stock B 6%. Moderate (0.50): A 9%, B 8%. Weak (0.20): A −6%, B 20%. What is the correlation between A and B?
keystrokes: Use the statistics (2nd DATA) or compute by hand: 0.3 × 9.3 × (−3.8) = −10.602

errors.label: Summed the deviation products without weighting by the probabilities
errors.explain: Each state's deviation product must be multiplied by its probability; an unweighted sum treats the states as equally likely.

errors.label: Reported the covariance (in decimals) as the correlation
errors.explain: The covariance still carries the units of σ_A σ_B; divide by σ_A σ_B to get ρ.

errors.label: Divided the covariance in %² by σ's in decimals
errors.explain: Mixing percent and decimal units gives a nonsense ρ far outside [−1, 1].

questions.explanation: ρ_AB = −0.95: the two stocks move almost exactly opposite across the three states, so a portfolio of both would remove most of the risk. Always compute E first, then deviations, then probability-weighted squares and products; a ρ outside [−1, 1] means a units slip.

questions.stem: In three equally likely states, Stock A returns 14%, 6% and −2%, while Stock B returns 3%, 7% and 11%. What is the correlation between A and B?
solution: ρ = −21.33/(6.532 × 3.266) = −1.00: B is an exact decreasing straight-line function of A (B falls 0.5 for every 1 that A rises)

errors.label: Reported the covariance (in decimals) as the correlation
errors.explain: A covariance of −0.0021 is not a correlation; divide by σ_A σ_B.

errors.label: Divided by σ_A² only (the slope of B on A)
errors.explain: Dividing by one variance gives a regression slope (−0.50), not the correlation, which divides by σ_A σ_B.

errors.label: Used Σ p R_A R_B instead of deviation products
errors.explain: Covariance is built from deviations from the means; E[R_A R_B] alone is not the covariance.

questions.explanation: ρ = −1.00 exactly: B is a perfect decreasing straight-line function of A. A perfectly negatively correlated pair is the strongest diversifier: the right weights make σ_P zero.

questions.stem: Over five years, Stock A returned 12%, −4%, 18%, 6% and 8%, and Stock B returned 5%, 9%, 1%, 7% and 3% (same years, same order). Using sample statistics (divide by N − 1), what is the correlation between A and B?
solution: Sum of products = 0 − 48 − 40 − 4 + 0 = −92, so cov = −92/4 = −23 %² = −0.0023 in decimals
keystrokes: 2nd DATA, enter X and Y pairs, 2nd STAT (LIN mode): Sx = 8.124, Sy = 3.162, r = −0.895

errors.label: Divided the covariance by N = 5 but the standard deviations by N − 1 = 4
errors.explain: All three quantities must use the same divisor; mixing N and N − 1 distorts ρ (here it shrinks it).

errors.label: Divided by σ_A² only (the slope of B on A)
errors.explain: Dividing by one variance gives a regression slope, not the correlation.

errors.label: Reported the covariance in decimals as the correlation
errors.explain: −0.0023 is a covariance; ρ needs the division by σ_A σ_B.

questions.explanation: With sample data use N − 1 throughout (and the same factor for cov, σ_A and σ_B): ρ ≈ −0.90. A strongly negative correlation means these two stocks are excellent diversifiers.

questions.stem: Over five years, Stock X returned 8%, 2%, 14%, 6% and 10%, and Stock Y returned 9%, 3%, 12%, 6% and 5% (same years, same order). Compute the sample covariance of their returns, entering returns as decimals (for example 8% = 0.08).

errors.label: Divided by N = 5 instead of N − 1 = 4
errors.explain: Five years of one stock's history is a sample: divide by N − 1.

errors.label: Worked in percent units: 52 %² ÷ 4
errors.explain: The question asks for decimals; 13 %² equals 0.0013 in decimal form.

errors.label: Did not divide the sum of products
errors.explain: A covariance is an average of the deviation products, so divide by N − 1.

questions.explanation: The sample covariance is Σ(R_X − mean)(R_Y − mean)/(N − 1) = 0.0052/4 = 0.0013 in decimals (13 in %² units). It is positive because the two stocks tended to be above or below their averages in the same years.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 20% and Stock B has σ = 25%, and the correlation between them is 0.4. What is the covariance of their returns, as a decimal?

errors.label: Multiplied the percentages directly (20 × 25 × 0.4)
errors.explain: σ must be written as decimals (0.20, 0.25); 200 is the covariance in %² units.

errors.label: Divided ρ by σ_A σ_B
errors.explain: ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B), so cov = ρ σ_A σ_B, not ρ ÷ (σ_A σ_B).

errors.label: Forgot one σ: ρ × σ_A
errors.explain: The covariance needs both standard deviations.

questions.explanation: cov(A,B) = ρ σ_A σ_B = 0.0200. This is the quantity you can drop straight into the covariance form of the portfolio variance: 2 w_A w_B cov(A,B).

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 14% and Stock B has σ = 10%; cov(A,B) = 0.0105 (decimals). What is the correlation between A and B?

errors.label: Reported the covariance as the correlation
errors.explain: The covariance is not bounded by ±1 and keeps squared-return units; divide by σ_A σ_B.

errors.label: Divided by σ_A² only
errors.explain: That is the slope of B on A (a beta-type number), not the correlation.

errors.label: Divided a decimal covariance by the σ product in percent (14 × 10)
errors.explain: Use decimals for both cov and σ (or percent for both).

questions.explanation: ρ = 0.0105/(0.14 × 0.10) = 0.75: a strong positive correlation, so the pair offers only a modest diversification benefit.

questions.stem: Stock A has σ = 16%. The covariance of A and B is 0.0156 (decimals) and their correlation is 0.65. What is Stock B's standard deviation (% per annum)?
solution: ρ = cov/(σ_A σ_B) rearranges to σ_A σ_B = cov/ρ = 0.0156/0.65 = 0.0240

errors.label: Ignored the correlation: cov ÷ σ_A
errors.explain: cov = ρ σ_A σ_B, so ρ must be divided out as well.

errors.label: Multiplied by ρ instead of dividing
errors.explain: ρ = cov/(σ_Aσ_B), so σ_B = cov/(ρ σ_A); ρ belongs in the denominator.

errors.label: Divided by ρ σ_A² (variance of A)
errors.explain: σ_A σ_B is a product of two standard deviations; only one is known, so divide by the known σ_A (not its square).

questions.stem: The diversification benefit of combining two stocks is best described as:
options: the amount by which σ_P falls below the weighted average of the stocks' σ's, available whenever ρ < 1
the higher expected return earned by holding two stocks instead of one
the complete elimination of risk once at least ten stocks are held
the risk reduction that occurs only when the stocks are negatively correlated
questions.explanation: The benefit is the gap between w_A σ_A + w_B σ_B (the ρ = 1 risk) and the actual σ_P. It exists for every ρ below 1, not only negative ones, it costs no expected return, and it never removes systematic risk.

questions.stem: A 50/50 mix of two stocks with σ = 15% and σ = 19% has a portfolio standard deviation of 13.1%. The gap between 13.1% and the weighted average of 17.0% is an illustration of:
options: a risk premium
domination
the diversification benefit
systematic risk
questions.explanation: The weighted average (17.0%) is what the portfolio would have if the stocks were perfectly correlated; the actual 13.1% is lower because ρ < 1. That shortfall is the diversification benefit.

questions.stem: On a risk-return diagram (σ on the horizontal axis, E[R] on the vertical axis), the curve traced by all mixes of two stocks bows to the left of the straight line joining them. What does this tell you about ρ_AB?
options: ρ_AB = 1: there is no diversification benefit
ρ_AB > 1: the portfolios are riskier than the stocks themselves
Nothing: the curve's shape depends only on the expected returns
ρ_AB < 1: the mixes are less risky than the weighted average of the two risks
questions.explanation: The straight line is the ρ = 1 case (σ_P is the weighted average of the σ's). Any curve bowed to the left means σ_P is below that line for the same expected return, so ρ < 1. The lower the correlation, the stronger the bow.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the set of two-stock portfolios on a risk-return diagram (σ on the horizontal axis)?
options: ρ = 1: a curve bowed to the left; ρ = 0: a straight line; ρ = −1: a straight line
ρ = 1: a straight line; ρ = 0: a curve bowed to the left; ρ = −1: two straight segments touching σ_P = 0
ρ = 1: two straight segments touching σ_P = 0; ρ = 0: a straight line; ρ = −1: a straight line
The shape is the same for every ρ; only the length of the curve changes
questions.explanation: At ρ = 1 risk is linear in the weights, so the mixes lie on a straight line. At ρ = 0 the curve bows to the left. At ρ = −1 the σ_P formula is a perfect square |w_A σ_A − w_B σ_B|, giving two straight segments that touch σ_P = 0 at the hedging weights.

questions.stem: In which of the following cases is there NO diversification benefit from mixing two stocks?
options: ρ_AB = 0
ρ_AB = +1
questions.explanation: A benefit exists whenever ρ < 1; it is just small when ρ is close to 1 (such as 0.95). Only perfect positive correlation makes σ_P exactly equal to the weighted average of the σ's.

questions.stem: Why does diversification reduce risk without reducing expected return?
options: Because diversified portfolios are always invested in the stock with the highest expected return
Because a lower correlation between the stocks raises the portfolio's expected return
Because E[R_P] is just a weighted average, while σ_P falls when the stocks do not move in lockstep
Because risk and return are unrelated for portfolios
questions.explanation: Return is linear in the weights (no correlation term) while risk is not. Lower correlation lowers σ_P but leaves E[R_P] untouched, so diversification is called the only 'free lunch' in finance (risk falls with no loss of expected return).

questions.stem: Why can adding a riskier stock (higher σ) to a portfolio lower the portfolio's standard deviation?
options: Because it cannot: adding a stock with a higher σ always raises σ_P
Because a low correlation lets its swings offset the rest of the portfolio's
Because a riskier stock always has a higher expected return that offsets the risk
Because the weights of the original stock increase
questions.explanation: For a small weight w in the new stock, the variance changes by roughly 2w times (ρ σ_new σ_old − σ_old²) plus an O(w²) term, so the change is negative when ρ < σ_old/σ_new. With σ_old = 10%, σ_new = 20% and ρ = 0.2 this holds, and σ_P falls.

questions.stem: You hold a portfolio and want to add one more stock. Candidates X and Y have the same expected return and the same σ. The correlation of X with your portfolio is 0.9 and of Y is 0.1. Which should you add, and why?
options: X, because a higher correlation means the stock behaves like what you know
Y, because its lower correlation gives a bigger fall in σ_P at the same expected return
Either, because stocks with equal E[R] and σ are interchangeable
X, because a stock that moves with the portfolio lowers its volatility
questions.explanation: At equal E[R] and σ, the better partner is the one with the lower ρ: its cross-term is smaller, so σ_P is lower. The professor's rule is 'for your next few stocks you want low ρ'.

questions.stem: Weights and standard deviations of two stocks are fixed, and the correlation between them rises from 0.2 to 0.8. What happens to the diversification benefit (weighted-average σ minus σ_P)?
options: It shrinks, because σ_P rises towards the unchanged weighted average
It grows, because a higher correlation means more co-movement
It is unchanged, because the weights and σ's are fixed
It becomes negative
questions.explanation: The weighted average of the σ's does not depend on ρ. σ_P increases with ρ, so the gap between them narrows; it reaches zero at ρ = 1. It never becomes negative for ρ ≤ 1.

questions.stem: With many stocks to choose from, the efficient frontier lies to the left of every individual stock on the risk-return diagram. What does this tell you?
options: Combinations achieve a lower σ for the same expected return than any single stock can
Individual stocks carry no risk of their own
The frontier is where expected returns are highest, whatever the risk
All stocks on the frontier are perfectly correlated with each other
questions.explanation: Individual stocks sit to the right of (or on) the frontier, so each is dominated by some combination: the same E[R] with lower σ. That is the diversification benefit seen across a universe of stocks.

questions.stem: On the two-stock curve (σ_P on the horizontal axis, E[R_P] on the vertical axis) with ρ_AB low enough for the curve to bend back, a point on the lower branch below the minimum-variance portfolio is:
options: efficient, because it has the highest weight in the riskier stock
the minimum-variance portfolio
the market portfolio
inefficient, because another mix has the same σ_P and a higher E[R_P]
questions.explanation: Points on the lower branch are dominated: moving up the curve to the other mix with the same σ_P raises E[R_P] at no extra risk. The lecture's point is that 'some weights are not efficient'.

questions.stem: A two-stock portfolio can have a standard deviation lower than that of either stock held alone.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. If ρ is low enough, mixing the stocks produces a minimum-variance portfolio whose σ_P is below both σ_A and σ_B (for example, ρ = −0.5 with equal σ's gives σ_P = 0.5 σ). It cannot happen at ρ = 1.

questions.stem: Diversification only reduces risk when the correlation between the stocks is negative.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Any ρ below +1 produces a diversification benefit (σ_P less than the weighted average of the σ's); negative correlation just makes it larger. At ρ = 0 and even at ρ = 0.5 risk still falls.

questions.stem: A two-stock portfolio gets a diversification benefit whenever the correlation between the stocks is _____ one.
options: less than
equal to
greater than
exactly zero or below
questions.explanation: σ_P equals the weighted average of the σ's only when ρ = 1, and it is lower for every ρ < 1. The benefit does not require ρ ≤ 0.

questions.stem: Two stocks, fixed 50/50 weights and fixed σ's, are combined under different correlations. Which ordering of σ_P, from largest to smallest, is correct?
options: All equal, because the weights and σ's are the same
questions.explanation: σ_P rises with ρ because only the cross-term 2ρ w_A σ_A w_B σ_B changes. The largest value is at ρ = +1, then 0.3, 0, and the smallest at −0.6.

questions.stem: A 50/50 portfolio combines Stock A (σ = 20%) and Stock B (σ = 30%) with a correlation of 0.25. By how many percentage points is the portfolio's standard deviation below the weighted average of the two standard deviations?
questions.explanation: Weighted average = 0.5(20) + 0.5(30) = 25%. σ_P = √(100 + 225 + 75) = √400 = 20%. Benefit = 25 − 20 = 5.00 percentage points. 20.00 is σ_P itself, 25.00 is the weighted average, and 6.97 uses ρ = 0 instead of 0.25.

questions.stem: A portfolio holds 60% of Stock A (σ = 28%) and 40% of Stock B (σ = 18%) with a correlation of 0.3. What percentage of the weighted-average risk is removed by diversification?
questions.explanation: Weighted average = 0.6(28) + 0.4(18) = 24.0%. σ_P = √(282.24 + 51.84 + 72.576) = √406.656 = 20.17%. Risk removed = (24.0 − 20.17)/24.0 = 15.98%. The alternatives give the share remaining (84.02%), the reduction in percentage points (3.83) and the reduction relative to σ_P (19.01%).

questions.stem: Stock C has σ = 26% and Stock D has σ = 14%; their correlation is 0.1. A portfolio holds 45% in C and 55% in D. How many percentage points below the weighted average of the two standard deviations is the portfolio's standard deviation?

errors.label: Reported σ_P itself instead of the gap
errors.explain: The question asks for the reduction relative to the weighted average, not the level of σ_P.

errors.label: Reported the weighted average
errors.explain: That is the risk at ρ = 1; the benefit is how far σ_P falls below it.

errors.label: Computed σ_P with ρ = 0 and took the gap
errors.explain: ρ = 0.1, not 0, so the cross-term must be included; ignoring it overstates the benefit.

questions.explanation: Diversification benefit = (w_C σ_C + w_D σ_D) − σ_P = 19.40% − 14.64% = 4.76 percentage points. The low ρ = 0.1 makes it large; at ρ = 1 it would be zero.

questions.stem: Two stocks each have σ = 24% and are held 50/50. By how many percentage points does the portfolio's standard deviation fall if the correlation between them drops from +0.5 to −0.5?

errors.label: Compared with ρ = 0 instead of −0.5
errors.explain: The question asks about ρ = −0.5, where the cross-term is negative (−72), not zero.

errors.label: Reported σ_P at ρ = −0.5
errors.explain: That is the level of risk at ρ = −0.5, not the fall from the ρ = +0.5 level.

errors.label: Subtracted the variances (432 − 144) and scaled
errors.explain: Take the square root of each variance before subtracting.

questions.explanation: Moving ρ from +0.5 to −0.5 lowers σ_P from 20.78% to 12.00%, a fall of 8.78 percentage points. Each step down in ρ shrinks the cross-term (+144, 0, −144) and with it σ_P.

questions.stem: You hold only Stock A (σ = 10%, E[R] = 6%). You move 20% of your money into the riskier Stock B (σ = 20%, E[R] = 11%). The correlation between A and B is 0.2. What is the new portfolio's standard deviation (% per annum)?

steps.label: Change in risk versus holding A alone (percentage points)

solution: σ_P = √92.8 = 9.63%, which is 0.37 percentage points below A's own 10%

errors.label: Weighted average of the SDs (12.0%)
errors.explain: That is the ρ = 1 answer and would wrongly suggest that adding a riskier stock raises risk.

errors.label: Dropped the cross-term (ρ = 0)
errors.explain: ρ = 0.2 adds 12.8 to the variance; ignoring it gives 8.94%, too low.

errors.label: Used 20% in A and 80% in B
errors.explain: The 80% weight belongs to Stock A (the stock you already hold).

questions.explanation: Even though B is twice as risky as A, a 20% slice lowers σ_P from 10.00% to 9.63% (and raises E[R_P] from 6% to 7%), because ρ = 0.2 is below σ_A/σ_B = 0.5. This is why holding only the lower-risk stock is inefficient.

questions.stem: Stock A (σ = 24%) and Stock B (σ = 16%) are perfectly negatively correlated (ρ = −1). What percentage of the portfolio should be in Stock A for the portfolio to have zero standard deviation?

steps.label: Sum of the two SDs, σ_A + σ_B

solution: With ρ = −1: σ_P = |w_A σ_A − w_B σ_B|, which is 0 when w_A σ_A = w_B σ_B

errors.label: Gave the weight to the other stock
errors.explain: The riskier stock needs the smaller weight so that the two weighted risks are equal.

errors.label: Used equal weights
errors.explain: Equal dollars give 0.5 × 24 = 12 against 0.5 × 16 = 8, which does not cancel.

errors.label: Used the ratio of the SDs
errors.explain: The weights must sum to 1, so w_A = σ_B/(σ_A + σ_B), not σ_B/σ_A.

questions.explanation: At ρ = −1 the risks cancel completely when w_A σ_A = w_B σ_B, giving w_A = σ_B/(σ_A + σ_B) = 40% (and 60% in B). This is the extreme diversification benefit: a riskless portfolio built from two risky stocks.

questions.stem: When the number of securities in a portfolio is increased, what typically happens to the standard deviation of the portfolio returns?
options: It decreases at an increasing rate
It increases at an increasing rate
It is unchanged
It decreases but at a decreasing rate
It increases but at a decreasing rate
questions.explanation: Adding securities averages out company-specific (diversifiable) risk, so the portfolio standard deviation falls; but each extra security removes less than the one before, and the fall levels off at the systematic (market) level σ_M. So σ_P decreases at a decreasing rate, not at an increasing rate and not all the way to zero.

questions.stem: Systematic risk is best defined as:
options: risk from economy-wide factors that diversification cannot remove
risk particular to one company or industry that disappears in a large portfolio
the standard deviation of a single stock's returns
the risk of holding fewer than ten securities
questions.explanation: Systematic (market, non-diversifiable) risk comes from economy-wide factors such as interest rates, inflation and GDP growth. Company-specific risk is the diversifiable part. Total σ of a stock includes both.

questions.stem: Equally weighted portfolios of randomly chosen Canadian stocks have an average standard deviation of 44% with 1 stock, 24% with 10, 20% with 100 and 19% with 1,000. The 19% or so that remains however many stocks are added is:
options: unsystematic (company-specific) risk
systematic (market) risk
diversifiable risk
the risk-free rate
questions.explanation: Diversification strips out company-specific risk, so the floor that remains is the market's own volatility σ_M: non-diversifiable, systematic risk.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a source of systematic risk?
options: A strike shuts down one company's only plant
A mining firm's chief executive resigns unexpectedly
The Bank of Canada unexpectedly raises its policy interest rate
A single restaurant chain recalls a contaminated product
questions.explanation: A policy-rate change affects the discount rates, borrowing costs and profits of almost every firm, so it cannot be diversified away. The other three events hit one firm only and tend to wash out in a diversified portfolio.

questions.stem: Which pairing of risk terms is correct?
options: Company-specific = non-diversifiable = systematic; market = diversifiable = non-systematic
Diversifiable = systematic; non-diversifiable = unsystematic
Company-specific = diversifiable = non-systematic; market = non-diversifiable = systematic
All of these terms are different names for total risk
questions.explanation: The professor's terminology: company-specific = diversifiable = non-systematic; market = non-diversifiable (undiversifiable) = systematic. Total risk = systematic + unsystematic.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT another name for systematic risk?
options: Market risk
Non-diversifiable risk
Undiversifiable risk
Company-specific risk
questions.explanation: Systematic risk is also called market risk, non-diversifiable and undiversifiable risk. Company-specific risk is its opposite: the diversifiable, non-systematic part.

questions.stem: Why can't holding more and more stocks eliminate systematic risk?
options: Because large portfolios have higher expected returns than small ones
Because systematic factors move almost all stocks the same way at once, so nothing offsets
Because systematic risk only affects the stocks that are not in the portfolio
Because adding stocks makes the correlation between them rise to zero
questions.explanation: Company-specific events offset because good news at one firm is unrelated to bad news at another. Economy-wide events (rates, recession) move nearly all firms together, so no number of stocks cancels them: σ_P levels off at the market volatility σ_M.

questions.stem: Why does the portfolio standard deviation fall at a decreasing rate as the number of stocks grows?
options: Because each added stock removes less of the specific risk that is left
Because later stocks have lower expected returns
Because each added stock has a larger weight than the previous one
Because the standard deviation falls at a constant rate until it reaches zero
questions.explanation: The second stock removes a large share of the diversifiable risk; by the tenth or thirtieth most of it is already gone, so extra stocks help little. What remains is the market volatility floor. In the textbook data, 10 stocks capture most of the benefit and 30 almost all of it.

questions.stem: Average standard deviations of equally weighted portfolios: 1 stock 44%, 2 stocks 33%, 5 stocks 27%, 10 stocks 24%, 30 stocks 21%, 100 stocks 20%. What does this pattern show?
options: Most of the reduction comes from the first few stocks; about 20% remains
Risk falls by about the same amount each time one more stock is added
Beyond 30 stocks the portfolio's risk starts to rise again
With 100 stocks all of the risk has been eliminated
questions.explanation: The drops shrink: 11 points from 1 to 2 stocks, but about 1 point from 30 to 100. The floor near 20% is the systematic risk that no number of stocks removes.

questions.stem: For a portfolio of randomly chosen stocks, as the number of stocks N becomes very large the standard deviation of the portfolio approaches:
options: zero
the average standard deviation of the individual stocks
σ_M, the volatility of the market (the systematic level)
the risk-free rate
questions.explanation: Unsystematic risk washes out, leaving the systematic component: σ_P tends to σ_M, not to zero and not to the average stock's σ.

questions.stem: By holding enough stocks, an investor can reduce the standard deviation of the portfolio's return to zero.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Diversification removes only the company-specific part; the market-wide (systematic) risk remains, so σ_P bottoms out near the market volatility σ_M (about 19-20% in the textbook data).

questions.stem: In a well-diversified portfolio, essentially all of the remaining risk is systematic.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. A well-diversified portfolio has almost no unsystematic risk left, so its total risk is essentially systematic; this is why β, not σ, becomes the relevant risk measure for an added stock in such a portfolio.

questions.stem: An investor holds all her savings in one Calgary oil producer. Which step reduces her total risk the most without necessarily lowering her expected return?
options: Buying a second Alberta oil producer with the same σ
Moving all of the money into the stock with the highest σ
Waiting for the oil price to rise before diversifying
Spreading the money over many stocks in different industries and countries
questions.explanation: Low-correlation holdings reduce company- and industry-specific risk. A second oil producer is highly correlated with the first, so it adds little; this follows the professor's rule: after the first stock, look for low ρ.

questions.stem: As more stocks are added, the portfolio standard deviation falls at a _____ rate towards the systematic level.
options: increasing
decreasing
constant
negative
questions.explanation: The fall is steep at first, then flattens: each additional stock removes less risk than the one before.

questions.stem: Which ordering of typical standard deviations, from largest to smallest, is correct for equally weighted portfolios of randomly chosen stocks?
options: One stock > 5 stocks > 30 stocks > broad market index
Broad market index > 30 stocks > 5 stocks > one stock
30 stocks > 5 stocks > one stock > broad market index
All are about equal because diversification cannot reduce σ
questions.explanation: σ falls as stocks are added and bottoms out at the market's volatility (the broad index is the limiting, fully diversified portfolio). A single stock carries all of its company-specific risk and has the largest σ.

questions.stem: With two stocks at ρ = −1 the portfolio risk can be driven to zero, yet no large portfolio of real stocks reaches zero. Why?
options: Real stocks all have the same expected return
Large portfolios always have weights larger than 1
The formula σ_P = w σ stops applying beyond two stocks
Real stocks share economy-wide factors, so a systematic floor remains
questions.explanation: ρ = −1 is an extreme two-stock case that real stocks never reach: nearly all stocks rise and fall with the market, so their correlations are positive on average. The economy-wide (systematic) part of their risk does not cancel, and σ_P levels off near the market's volatility σ_M.

questions.stem: A portfolio of 25 randomly chosen TSX stocks has σ = 20.3%, while the broad TSX index has σ = 18.9%. What does the 1.4-point gap suggest?
options: The 25-stock portfolio must already lie on the efficient frontier
Adding another 25 stocks would roughly halve the portfolio's σ
Little more risk can be removed: what remains of the 25-stock risk is mostly systematic
The index must contain more unsystematic risk than the portfolio
questions.explanation: The portfolio is already within 1.4 points of the market's own volatility, so the only risk left to remove is the small unsystematic slice. Doubling the number of stocks would shave off at most a fraction of that 1.4 points.

questions.stem: A single randomly chosen stock has a standard deviation of 48.0%, while an equally weighted portfolio of 10 such stocks has a standard deviation of 26.4%. What percentage of the single stock's standard deviation is removed by holding the 10-stock portfolio?
questions.explanation: Reduction = (48.0 − 26.4)/48.0 = 21.6/48.0 = 45.00%. The 55.00% option is the share that remains, 26.40 is the level of σ_P rather than a reduction, and 181.82% inverts the ratio.

questions.stem: Typical standard deviations of equally weighted portfolios of Canadian large caps are 40.0% for one stock, 22.0% for ten stocks, 18.4% for forty stocks, and 16.0% for the whole market. What percentage of the maximum possible risk reduction (from one stock down to the market level) is achieved by holding ten stocks?

steps.label: Maximum possible reduction (one stock to market)
Share of the possible reduction achieved

errors.label: Divided by the single stock's σ instead of the reducible amount
errors.explain: The market floor (16%) cannot be diversified away, so the benchmark is the 24-point reducible part, not all 40 points.

errors.label: Gave the share still to be removed
errors.explain: That is the remaining part (25%); the question asks what has been achieved.

errors.label: Divided the portfolio's σ by the single stock's σ
errors.explain: That is the ratio of risks (55%), not the share of the reducible risk achieved.

questions.explanation: Ten stocks remove 18 of the 24 points that diversification can ever remove: 75%. This is the textbook's point that 'by the time we have 10 securities, most of the effect is already realized'. The last 6 points need dozens more stocks.

questions.stem: A portfolio's standard deviation is 49.0% with 1 stock, 37.0% with 2, 30.0% with 4 and 25.2% with 8. How many times larger is the reduction from adding the second stock than the average reduction per added stock when going from 4 to 8 stocks?

steps.label: Average reduction per stock from 4 to 8 (points)

solution: Adding the 2nd stock: 49.0 − 37.0 = 12.0 points for one stock
From 4 to 8 stocks: (30.0 − 25.2)/4 = 1.2 points per added stock

errors.label: Used the whole 4-to-8 reduction (4.8) instead of the per-stock average
errors.explain: Four stocks were added between 4 and 8, so divide the 4.8-point fall by 4.

errors.label: Inverted the ratio
errors.explain: The question asks how many times larger the early gain is, not the reverse.

errors.label: Used the 2-to-4 average (3.5) as the comparison
errors.explain: The comparison interval is 4 to 8 stocks.

questions.explanation: The second stock cuts σ by 12 points, but each of the stocks added between 4 and 8 cuts it by only 1.2 on average: ten times less. That is 'a decreasing rate' in numbers.

questions.stem: In the textbook's data, a randomly chosen single stock has an average σ of 49.24%, a 30-stock portfolio 20.87%, and a 1,000-stock portfolio 19.21%. What percentage of the total diversification achieved by 1,000 stocks is already achieved by 30 stocks?

errors.label: Divided the 30-stock reduction by the single stock's σ
errors.explain: That ignores that 19.21 points of σ can never be diversified away.

errors.label: Divided the 30-stock σ by the single-stock σ
errors.explain: That is the ratio of risk levels (42%), not the share of the reduction achieved.

errors.label: Compared the 30-stock σ with the 1,000-stock σ
errors.explain: That gives 92%, the ratio of the two floors, not the share of the diversification achieved.

questions.explanation: Thirty stocks already deliver 94.47% of everything diversification can do; the other 970 stocks add the last 5.53%. This is the 'decreasing rate' and 'limit at σ_M' pattern: 'by the time we get to 30 or so, there is little remaining benefit' (Ross).
